for (label in c("data", "data-code-archiving-counts", "full-317-audit-load")) {

}

# Detailed record of every Metacheck defect found and fixed during this project {#apx-defects}

This appendix documents, in full detail and in chronological order, every software defect in Metacheck that this project's validation effort identified, the evidence that surfaced each one, the exact code change that fixed it, and the corpus-level numbers before and after that fix. The body of the manuscript reports only the final, current numbers; this appendix exists so that every intermediate claim made in the course of arriving at those numbers remains checkable, without requiring the main text to carry a running commentary on its own revision history. Seven rounds of validation are documented below: (A.1) the original empirical-comparison review against Cooper et al.'s coding, which produced issues #378–#384; (A.2) a focused re-examination of `code_check`'s parse-error and package-version-pinning checks; (A.3) a systematic validation of five further `code_check` checks (missing referenced files, hardcoded absolute paths, `setwd()` calls, comment density, and library/import scattering) against real corpus files, which produced five further fixes; (A.4) a file-count gate added after one outlier repository's processing time exposed a gap the existing byte-size caps did not cover; (A.5) a full re-check of every remaining disagreement against Metacheck after five more fixes (Zenodo reliability, repository-platform coverage, and a rate-limit reliability defect found live during the re-check itself); (A.6) a systemic under-sampling bug found in A.5's own Dataverse DOI-prefix allowlist, two further platform-coverage fixes (DataONE, institutional Figshare instances) and two matching bugs in this project's own comparison code, and a complete, evidence-based categorization of every "repository not detected" disagreement these fixes did not resolve; and (A.7) a full-corpus run of Metacheck's `reproducibility_check` module — a different question from A.1–A.6 (does a paper's own shared code actually run and reproduce its own reported results, not merely whether a repository was detected) — which surfaced five further defects specific to running many papers' Docker containers concurrently at corpus scale and to extracting a paper's own declared dependencies from its code. Fixes described in A.1–A.4 were committed to `scienceverse/metacheck`, branch `repocheck_improvements` (pull request #385); A.5 and A.6's fixes were committed directly to that package's `dev` branch (A.6 as pull requests #410, #412, and #414); A.7's five defects were filed as issues #417–#421, two of which (#419, #420) are confirmed fixed on `dev` as of this writing. Every fix from A.1–A.6 is covered by a new or updated automated regression test in the package's own test suite; A.7's two confirmed-fixed defects were fixed and committed by the package's maintainer rather than by this project directly, so this manuscript does not independently confirm test coverage for them.

## A.1 Defects found during the original empirical comparison

Six defects were identified while individually reviewing every disagreement between Metacheck and Cooper et al.'s human coding (Empirical Comparison, above): five in Metacheck itself, and one in this project's own comparison code. All six are described here with the same level of detail as in the body text; they are repeated in this appendix only for completeness, so that Appendix A is a single, complete record of every fix made during this project.

**#378 — `zip_peek()`'s unauthenticated requests.** `zip_peek()` (`R/zip-peek.R`) reads a remote zip archive's central directory via an HTTP Range request, without downloading the archive, so a downloader can decide whether the archive is worth fetching before spending the bandwidth. This function's HEAD and Range requests were unauthenticated. Dryad's file-download endpoint answers 401 Unauthorized to *any* request that touches file bytes, including a bare HTTP Range request — confirmed live against a real Dryad file-download URL — so every Dryad-hosted archive's peek failed structurally, before any question of the archive's actual contents. Fix: both requests now route through `.auth_for_url()`, the same host-based authentication dispatcher every other Metacheck download path already uses, so Dryad's token is attached automatically without requiring each call site to opt in individually (an earlier, per-call-site `req_func` opt-in mechanism had only been adopted by 1 of 7 call sites that needed it).

**#379 — `data_check`'s multi-sheet Excel limitation.** `data_check`'s tabular-usability check called `readxl::read_excel()` with no `sheet` argument, so it only ever read a workbook's first sheet. When the first sheet was a cover, metadata, or "read me" sheet — a convention confirmed across many real corpus files, with sheet names including "metadata," "Meta-data," "MetaData," "read me," "ReadMe," "User guide," "LEGEND," and "Description of variables" — a later sheet holding genuine, well-structured tabular data was never inspected, and the file was misclassified as unusable ("100% free text, not variables"). One confirmed case: sheet 2 of a real downloaded workbook held 1,532 rows by 58 real variable columns, never read before the fix. Fix: `data_read_head()` now accepts a `sheet` argument, and `data_check` tries each remaining sheet in a workbook before giving up on the file. This was the single largest driver of `data_download` disagreement: before the fix, `mc_data_download` and Cooper et al.'s `data_download` disagreed on 51 of 967 comparable papers (94.7% agreement); after it, agreement rose to 99.1% (908/916 papers, 8 disagreements remaining), and the resolved cases accounted for 29 of the original 51 disagreements (57%).

**#380 — Dryad's authentication gap on other download paths.** The same unauthenticated-request problem identified for `zip_peek()` (#378) also affected `.remote_size()` and `.remote_content_length()`, two other functions in the download path that check a remote file's size via HTTP HEAD before deciding whether and how to download it. `.remote_content_length()` already had a `req_func` opt-in mechanism for per-host authentication, but only 1 of 7 call sites across the codebase had actually adopted it, so the other 6 still received a 401 from Dryad. Fix: both functions now route through `.auth_for_url()` unconditionally, the same fix applied to #378, closing every remaining unauthenticated-request gap in the download path at once rather than patching call sites one at a time.

**#383 — `code_check` could not see code bundled inside a zip archive.** This was a compound architectural gap with three separate causes, discovered while investigating why `code_check` found no code files at all for several papers whose repository, on manual inspection, clearly contained real analysis scripts bundled inside a `.zip`: (1) `code_check()` never read `data_check`'s already-expanded file structure, so any code file `data_check` had already discovered inside a zip (in the course of looking for data files) was invisible to `code_check` regardless; (2) `code_check` had no zip-peek capability of its own for the case where `data_check` had not already run first; (3) the shared zip-expansion helper `.archive_rows()` discarded code-typed files outright even when it did expand a zip, keeping only `"data"` and `"documentation"`-typed files. Fix: `code_check()` now prefers `data_check`'s structure when available; it gets its own zip-peek fallback (`.code_expand_zip()`) for when `data_check` did not run first; and `.archive_rows()` now keeps `"code"` alongside `"data"`/`"documentation"`. A real, concrete example verified live: a Zenodo record (record 3694205, repository `SharpRT/CMV_Spread`) bundled 4 real MATLAB `.m` files inside a zip that were entirely invisible to `code_check` before this fix. This fix, together with the archive-member content-fetch wiring described immediately below, moved `code_download` agreement from 66.2% (355 comparable papers, 120 disagreements) to 89.7% (358 comparable papers, 37 disagreements) — the first of two stages in this construct's improvement (the second is #384, below).

As part of the same round of work, `repo_check`'s zip-peek expansion was extended to carry not just a discovered code file's *name* (already possible after the fixes above) but its *content*: each expanded row now also carries `archive_url` (the parent zip's own URL) and `archive_member` (the file's exact name inside it), and `download_repo_files()` (`R/repo-download.R`) uses those two fields to fetch that one member's bytes directly, via a byte-range request against the parent archive, without downloading the archive's other contents. This mechanism was verified working in every isolated unit test at the time, but a full end-to-end pipeline run against a real paper still returned no file content for reasons not yet diagnosed at that point — this was filed and tracked as issue #384, described next, rather than merged as "fixed" while a known gap remained open.

**#384 — Two distinct causes behind the archive-member byte-fetch failing intermittently.** Issue #384 was filed as an open question ("archive-member content fetch works in isolation but returned NA once in a full pipeline run") rather than a diagnosed bug, and its investigation spanned two separate validation efforts and uncovered two independent causes.

*Cause 1: silent truncation over 32,768 bytes.* `.zip_inflate_member()` (`R/zip-peek.R`) decompresses one zip member's raw bytes by calling `zip::inflate()`. Passing the member's exact known uncompressed size to that function raised an unrelated "Failed to inflate data" error (a quirk internal to the `zip` package), so the original code left the `size` argument unset instead. `zip::inflate()`'s own documentation states that leaving `size` unset triggers automatic buffer resizing as needed — but, confirmed live against a real Zenodo-hosted zip member, this documented behaviour does not actually happen in practice: any member larger than the default 32,768-byte output buffer came back silently truncated at exactly that length, with no error, no warning, and a `bytes_written` field the calling code never inspected. A concrete confirmed case: a real 44,669-byte code file came back as exactly 32,768 bytes. `.zip_member_fetch()`'s own subsequent length check (comparing the decompressed length against the size recorded in the archive's own central directory) correctly caught this mismatch and discarded the truncated bytes — but the practical, user-visible effect was that every code or data file over 32KB inside a zip silently failed to fetch, indistinguishable from a genuine network or host-compatibility failure. Fix: passing `size + 1` (one byte over the true size) avoids both failure modes — it is no longer the exact size that triggers the package's internal error, and it is large enough that the real output always fits in the up-front buffer rather than depending on the documented-but-non-functional resize path. Verified against both a real archive member under 32KB and one over it, and covered by a new offline regression test using a locally constructed zip file whose one member compresses to roughly 95KB uncompressed. A targeted rerun of the 36 papers affected by this pattern found 27 moved from zero downloadable code files to full or near-full recovery (23 fully, 4 partially), which is what raised `code_download` agreement from 89.7% (37 disagreements) to 97.2% (10 disagreements remaining) — the second of the two stages in this construct's improvement, and the largest single agreement-rate improvement of any construct in the empirical comparison.

*Cause 2: an intermittent, silently-swallowed failure not explained by the truncation bug alone.* Independently of the truncation bug, a second cause was found while investigating why 40 of the archives affected by issue #384 failed *entirely* (every member missing) despite containing no member anywhere near the 32,768-byte threshold. Tracing the actual corpus data (`res_code_check.RData` and its 38 per-batch constituent files, in `cooper_validation_metacheck/manuscript/data/`) showed that a single pipeline run calls `zip_peek()` on the exact same archive URL *twice* — once inside `repo_check` to discover a zip's member names, and again inside `download_repo_files()`'s archive-member-fetch step (added as part of #383/#384's own fix) to retrieve one member's bytes — with no throttling and, critically, no retry logic at all on either call: `zip_peek()`'s own HEAD request and its two Range-request helper functions (`.http_range_tail()`, `.http_range_bytes()`) called `httr2::req_perform()` directly, with no `req_retry()`, and treated *any* non-206/200 HTTP status (including a 429 burst-rate-limit refusal) as an unconditional, silent `NULL` — indistinguishable, by design, from "this host does not support range requests at all." Two back-to-back, unthrottled requests to the same archive URL within one process is exactly the pattern most likely to trip a host's burst-rate limiter, and the *second* call (the byte-fetch, inside `download_repo_files()`) was the one exposed to it. Fix, applied in two parts: (1) all three of `zip_peek()`'s network calls now retry through the same `is_transient`/`backoff`/rate-limit-wait helper functions (`.storage_is_transient_factory()`, `.storage_backoff()`, `.storage_retry_after_factory()`) that every other Metacheck download path already uses, so a 429 is now retried with backoff rather than immediately and silently treated as "unsupported"; (2) a new same-session, in-memory cache (`.zip_peek_cache`, keyed by URL) means the second call to `zip_peek()` on an archive already peeked earlier in the same run reuses the first call's result instead of repeating the network request at all, removing the redundant call — and the rate-limit exposure it caused — entirely rather than merely tolerating it. Verified by a new regression test exercising the cache directly (`test-zip-peek.R`) and by the full package test suite (463 tests passing, 3 pre-existing unrelated skips, 0 failures) after both changes.

**Verdict corrections found by the post-rerun double-check pass.** After the full corpus rerun incorporating #378–#384, every disagreement was independently double-checked a second time (see Empirical Comparison, above, for the check's method). This pass corrected 7 verdict-labeling errors from the original review: 2 in `data_availability` (one moved to `COOPER_RIGHT` after finding the "data" files actually belonged to a cited third-party software dependency's repository, not the paper's own; one moved to `METACHECK_RIGHT` after finding a methods paper's repository, originally read as containing only package example files, in fact holds real trait data and model output), 1 in `data_download` (moved to `COOPER_RIGHT` after confirming a Zenodo-hosted "Functional Trait Database" file had, in fact, already downloaded and still failed the tabular-usability check, rather than remaining `UNCLEAR` on the assumption it had not yet downloaded), and 4 in `code_download` (three rows originally recorded `METACHECK_RIGHT` whose own written reasoning already concluded the opposite, corrected to `COOPER_RIGHT`; one row originally left `UNCLEAR` where the code files were, on direct inspection, confirmed genuinely downloaded, corrected to `METACHECK_RIGHT`). The pass also found one substantial scope correction rather than a single-row relabeling: `code_download`'s dominant post-#383 disagreement pattern was originally tagged in only 13 of its 37 disagreements at the time of the initial qualitative review; re-deriving the pattern systematically against every disagreement's saved `file_location` value found the identical signature (a discovered code file with no resolvable download location) in 35 of the 37, which is what led directly to tracing and fixing #384's second cause, above. Every one of `code_archived`'s 164 disagreements was also individually re-derived against the current `repo_check`/`code_check` file listing during this pass, including the 8 originally resolved via an automated keyword search rather than an individual hand read; this found zero verdict corrections in that column.

**A sixth issue, not in Metacheck but in this project's own comparison code.** `code_data_preparation/03_recreate_cooper_columns.R` derives `mc_data_availability`, `mc_code_archived`, `mc_data_README`, and `mc_code_README` for a paper from `repo_check`'s per-*file* tables (`res_repo_check$table`, `res_data_check$structure`, `res_code_check$table`). A paper for which `repo_check` found zero files anywhere has no row at all in any of those three tables, even though `repo_check`'s own per-paper `summary_table` — which covers every one of the 1861 papers — correctly records `files_n = 0` for it. Because the script built its paper list from the three per-file tables rather than from `summary_table`, every such paper was silently absent from the comparison entirely: its `mc_*` value was not `FALSE`, it simply never existed as a row to compare. Confirmed directly: 495 of 1861 papers were missing this way, including 404 papers Cooper et al. coded `data_availability` `Yes` — 404 real disagreements (cases where Cooper et al.'s coders found a repository Metacheck's own detection had missed) that were never entering the comparison at all, rather than being counted as a genuine miss. Fix: the paper list is now built from `summary_table$paper_id` (already the full 1861 by construction), and `mc_data_availability`, `mc_code_archived`, `mc_data_README`, and `mc_code_README` are explicitly set to `FALSE` for a paper `repo_check` examined and found nothing in; every other `mc_*` column (license, DOI, download, format, language) is correctly left `NA` for such a paper, since those questions remain genuinely inapplicable without a repository to ask about. Every number reported in the Empirical Comparison section above reflects this correction.

## A.2 Re-examining `code_check`'s parse-error and package-version-pinning numbers

A separate line of inquiry, prompted directly by a sentence in an earlier manuscript draft stating that "138 files (1.3%) failed to parse as valid code in their declared language at all," asked two questions: is this the right denominator, and is the file list behind it available for inspection at all.

**Locating the underlying data.** `code_check()`'s per-run output already carries everything needed: a `table` with one row per code file (`file_name`, `language`, `parse_error`, `parse_error_msg`) and a `summary_table` with one row per *paper* (`code_version_pinned`, `code_parse_errors`), both already computed by the module — no new code was needed to make this data available, only to locate and aggregate the 38 saved per-batch corpus-run files (`cooper_validation_metacheck/manuscript/data/batches/res_code_check_batch001.RData` through `batch038.RData`) that had already been produced by the original corpus run.

**Package version pinning: 34.2% was a batch-level upper bound, not a per-paper rate.** An earlier manuscript draft reported that "only 13 of 38 batches (34.2%) contain at least one paper with any form of version pinning," explicitly flagged in that draft's own text as an upper bound on the true per-paper rate because a batch of ~50 papers needs only one pinned paper to count. Checking directly against the saved per-batch `summary_table$code_version_pinned` column (present in every batch, keyed by `paper_id`) confirmed the per-paper detail this draft believed was not retained had, in fact, been retained all along: aggregating it across all 38 batches gives 18 of 400 code-bearing papers (4.5%) with version pinning present — substantially lower than the 34.2% upper bound, as expected, and now a true per-paper number rather than an aggregate-of-aggregates. No code fix was needed here; this was a reporting correction (using data that already existed but had not yet been extracted at the right level of granularity), not a software defect.

**Parse errors: 1.3% used the wrong denominator, and undercounted for a subtler reason.** The originally reported 1.3% divided 138 parse failures by 10,461, the total code-file count across *every* language in the corpus — but parsing is only ever attempted on R-type files (`.R`, `.Rmd`, `.qmd`; `code_parse_r()` is R-only), so the other 3,259 SAS/SPSS/Stata/Python/MATLAB files in the corpus were never eligible to fail this check and should not have been in the denominator at all. Restricting to the corpus's 7,202 R-type files, a further complication emerged: 1,651 of those were never actually downloaded or read at all (an inaccessible repository or a failed download), so parsing was never attempted on them either — they, too, do not belong in the denominator. A further 15 files reached a local copy but errored during *extraction* (before `parse()` itself was ever called), splitting into two genuinely different causes on closer inspection: 11 were confirmed to be genuinely empty (0-byte) files — fetched directly from their original GitHub repositories to confirm the emptiness is a fact about the authors' own repository, not an artefact of Metacheck's download step (e.g. `github.com/olgaviedma/LadderFuelsR`'s `R/foofy.R` and `github.com/dpritchard/frair`'s `tests/testthat/test_emdII.R`, both independently confirmed 0 bytes via a direct `curl` fetch from `raw.githubusercontent.com`) — and 3 were `.Rmd` files that failed during Quarto/knitr's own chunk-extraction step with a genuine, structural fence-mismatch error (a closing code-fence with a different number of backticks or indentation than its opening fence), which is the same underlying "not valid in its declared format" problem a parse error represents, just caught one step earlier in the pipeline than `parse()` itself. Restricting to the 5,536 files that were both locally available and actually reached a call to `parse()`, 138 failed (2.5%) — not 1.3%, and not the 1.92% that a denominator of "all 7,202 R-type files regardless of whether they were ever read" would give either. Including the 3 fence-mismatch failures as the same kind of problem gives 141 of 5,539 (2.5%).

This investigation also surfaced a genuine, previously unknown software defect: **`code_read()` (`R/code_check.R`) crashes on a genuinely empty file.** `readr::guess_encoding()` returns a zero-row result for a 0-byte file, so `enc <- readr::guess_encoding(file_path)$encoding[[1]]` silently produces `NA` rather than a valid encoding string, and that `NA` then crashes deep inside `readr`'s own internals (`if (stringi::stri_enc_isascii(lines))`, which requires a length-one logical and receives `NA` instead) with the unhelpful, generic message `"missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed"` — this is exactly the message recorded for all 11 of the empty-file cases above, rather than a clear "this file is empty" signal. This defect affected a small fraction of files (11 of 7,202 R-type files in this corpus) and was not fixed during the review described here; it has since been fixed: in Metacheck 0.3.3.11, `code_read()` returns an empty result for a 0-byte file instead of failing (checked directly on 18 October 2026).

## A.3 Systematic validation of five further `code_check` checks

A third, more systematic validation exercise checked five of `code_check`'s remaining automated checks — missing referenced files, hardcoded absolute paths, `setwd()` calls, comment density, and scattered library/import lines — against real files from the same corpus, reading every flagged file that had already been downloaded locally (8,218 of 10,461 code-file rows) and sampling up to 100 of the remainder that would have required a fresh download. The full method, every sampled file's judgment, and every quoted example are recorded in a dedicated, reproducible validation report (`code_check_validation.qmd`, with its accompanying script `validate_code_check.R` and judgment tables, all in `cooper_validation_metacheck/manuscript/`) with a fixed random seed (`set.seed(42)`) at every sampling step; this appendix summarizes its findings and the resulting code fixes. Two checks not covered by this validation pass (parse errors, package version pinning) are covered separately in A.2 above.

**Missing referenced files — case-sensitivity bug (fixed).** `code_check`'s check for files a script tries to open but that are absent from the repository (`inst/modules/code_check.R`, `missing_files <- setdiff(base_ref, base_repo)`) compared filenames case-sensitively. 13 confirmed false positives across the sampled files were all the same mechanism: the referenced file exists in the repository under a different letter case, which is not a real error on the author's part on the case-insensitive filesystems (Windows, macOS by default) most authors develop on. Concrete examples, each confirmed directly against the paper's real repository file listing: paper `10_1002_2688_8319_12229` references `REM_tools.r` where the repository holds `REM_tools.R`; paper `10_1111_2041_210x_13923` references `diagnostic_fcns.r`/`boot_glmm.r` where the repository holds `diagnostic_fcns.R`/`boot_glmm.R`; paper `10_1111_2041_210x_13125` references `FoodWeb_Functions.R` where the repository holds `Foodweb_functions.R`; paper `10_1002_pan3_10736` references two scripts whose repository copies differ only in the first letter's case. Fix: the comparison now lowercases both sides before comparing (`missing_files <- base_ref[!tolower(base_ref) %in% tolower(base_repo)]`), removing all 13 confirmed false positives found in this sample and any of the same kind not yet sampled.

**Missing referenced files — `vroom::vroom()` not recognised as a file-reading call (fixed).** The same check's file-reference extractor (`code_file_refs()`, `R/code_check.R`) recognises a fixed list of R reader-function names (`read.*`/`read_*`, `import`, `fread`, `readRDS`, `load`, `readLines`, `fromJSON`, `readtext`, `source`); `vroom::vroom()` does not begin with "read" and was absent from this list, so a file loaded exclusively via `vroom::vroom()` was invisible to the missing-file check regardless of whether it actually existed in the repository. Confirmed false negative: paper `10_1111_2041_210x_13440`'s `R/ncbi.R` calls `vroom::vroom(file.path(dir, "nodes.dmp"), ...)` and a second `vroom::vroom()` call for `names.dmp`; neither file exists in the repository, but the check never flagged either, since `vroom` was not on its keyword list. Fix: `"vroom"` added to the reader-keyword list.

**Missing referenced files — remaining known limitations, not yet fixed.** Two further false-negative mechanisms were confirmed but not fixed, since each would require a more substantial change than a keyword addition or a comparison tweak: (1) `code_file_refs()` only captures a quoted filename appearing on the *same line* as a reader-call keyword, so a file assigned to a variable on one line and read via that variable on a later line (`liz_file <- "example_lizard_data.csv"`, then later `read.csv(liz_file)`) is invisible to the check even when the file genuinely does not exist (confirmed: paper `10_1111_1365_2435_13993`'s `tests/testthat/test-m_run_biophysical.R` does exactly this for three files, none of which exist in the repository). (2) When a referenced filename is built as `paste0(some_variable, "...literal_suffix.csv")`, the check's regex only captures the literal trailing fragment (e.g. `_M_D_abundance_interactions.csv`) rather than the true, variable-interpolated filename — the resulting "missing file" flag is still technically correct (nothing by that literal fragment name exists either), but the name shown to a paper's author is a confusing partial match rather than the file they would recognise; across the corpus, 128 of 2,599 (4.9%) genuinely-missing entries have a name starting with punctuation, the signature of this dropped-prefix pattern.

**Hardcoded absolute paths — three false-positive mechanisms fixed, one left open.** `code_abs_path()` (`R/code_check.R`) regex-matches quoted strings shaped like an absolute filesystem path. Three confirmed false-positive mechanisms were fixed: (1) a single-segment string beginning with `/` (e.g. `self.fetch('/login')` in a vendored web-app test suite, `github.com_ccrisan_motioneye/tests/test_handlers/test_login.py`) is an HTTP route, not a filesystem path — 322 of 4,182 originally matched strings were 6 characters or fewer, a class dominated by exactly this pattern; the regex's bare-`/`-prefixed branch now requires a second `/`-separated segment before matching, which a real absolute path (e.g. `/Users/name`) always has and a bare route never does. (2) An all-digit UNC "host" is a `sub()`/`gsub()` regex backreference string, not a network path — confirmed twice in real code: `osf.io_5fter/IDcallR_sameN_withIDcallPP.R` line 183, `sub('group (\d+)_(\d+)', "\2\1", colnames(clupo))`, where `"\2\1"` was matched as `\\host\share` because a bare digit satisfied the old hostname character class; and a second, independent instance in a Pyrenees-mapping script's `gsub('(.{1,10})(\s|$)', '\1\n', ...)` call, matched for the same reason. The UNC branch's hostname character class now requires at least one letter, which excludes both confirmed cases without excluding any real hostname (no genuine UNC host is all-digit-and-punctuation with no letter at all). (3) The pattern's own pre-existing docstring already flagged a known risk — a variable-built path like `paste0(dir, '/file.csv')` triggering a false match on the literal fragment — and this was confirmed for real: `github.com_YvesBas_Tadarida-C/Sonotypes/write_tabase3HF_Sonotype.R` line 40, `list.files(paste(ListDate[[i]],"/eti",sep=""), ...)`, where `"/eti"` is a relative fragment concatenated onto a loop variable. This third mechanism is addressed by the same "require a second path segment" fix as (1), since `/eti` is itself single-segment. A fourth mechanism, confirmed but **not fixed**: a Python string built by `+`-concatenation from a relative literal (`'data\\' + tile_name + '\\run\\' + model_name + ...`, from a Zenodo-hosted `model_test.py`) is a relative path whose middle segments (`\run\`, `\output\tile\`) still match the UNC branch on their own; no fully static regex-only fix exists for this case, since it would require tracking whether the enclosing expression is a string concatenation starting with a relative literal, which is beyond what a line-based regex can determine. Of the true positives sampled for comparison, 15 of 15 further-checked "real username-shaped" matches (e.g. `C:/Users/reddin/Documents/...`, `/Users/farrer/Dropbox/...`, `/home/michael/Dropbox/...`) were confirmed genuine, machine-specific absolute paths — the large majority of this check's flags are correct.

**`setwd()` calls — no false positives found in this corpus; one confirmed-but-unobserved risk noted.** All 194 distinct `setwd()` call strings found across the sampled files are genuine, live, executable calls, including calls whose argument is itself relative or dynamic (`setwd("./data")`, `setwd(dir)`, `setwd(tempdir())`) — these correctly count as flags under this check's own stated rule, since the anti-pattern being flagged is changing the working directory at all, not specifically a hardcoded absolute-path argument. A latent false-positive mechanism was confirmed by construction (a synthetic test, not a real corpus case): `code_setwd()` has no awareness of string-literal context, so a line like `message("Please run setwd(your_path) before continuing")` would be matched as if it were a live call. Scanning all 194 real call strings in the corpus for instructional-text markers ("please," "before," "instructions," "note:") found zero real occurrences of this pattern — a real, demonstrated risk with no confirmed instance in this corpus, and left unfixed for that reason, though `code_setwd()` could straightforwardly reuse the same quote-context-tracking logic already implemented for `.code_strip_inline_comment()` if a future corpus surfaces a real case.

**Comment density — a Python-specific docstring signal added (not a bug fix).** `code_remove_comments()`'s Python branch deliberately never treats a triple-quoted string as a comment, since doing so would also destroy real docstrings (themselves ordinary string literals, syntactically). The consequence, quantified directly: of 280 zero-comment-flagged Python files in the corpus, 200 (71.4%) contain at least one complete triple-quoted docstring block — real documentation that the mechanical `#`-only comment count cannot see, and so reports as "0% comments" regardless. Five were read directly to confirm these are genuine module/function docstrings rather than incidental triple-quoted data, e.g. `model_runs.py`'s `"""Filters for Model Runs."""` and `features.py`'s 16 separate triple-quote markers (8 docstrings) opening with `"""API functions to interact with feature names."""`. This is a deliberate, correctly-reasoned design choice in `code_remove_comments()`, not a bug — stripping docstrings to count them as comments would also delete them from every downstream check that reads code text — so the fix made is additive rather than corrective: a new function, `.code_has_docstring()`, detects whether a file contains at least one complete triple-quoted block, and `code_line_stats()` now returns this as a separate `has_docstring` field (`NA` for every non-Python language) alongside the unchanged `percent_comments` metric. `inst/modules/code_check.R`'s report text now adds an explanatory note whenever a zero-comment Python file in fact has a docstring, so a reader is told the file is documented via docstrings rather than concluding it has no documentation at all.

**Scattered library/import lines — Python import-anchor tightened (fixed).** `code_library_lines()` (`R/code_check.R`) previously anchored its Python import-detection regex on the bare keyword plus a following word (`^\s*(import|from)\s+[A-Za-z_.]`), with no requirement that the rest of the line actually form a valid import statement. Because Python's comment-removal never strips triple-quoted strings (the same mechanism behind the comment-density finding immediately above), docstring *prose* that happens to start with "from " or "import " survives into this scan and was matched as if it were a real import line. Concrete, exact example: `github.com_openvinotoolkit_cvat/site/process_sdk_docs.py`, line 213, inside a docstring spanning lines 211–214 — the prose sentence "        from the generated model and api descriptions." was matched as an import line at line 154 of the comment-stripped text, while the file's 10 real imports are all genuinely contiguous at lines 1–10; the spurious match alone widened the reported gap between imports to 144 lines, crossing the "scattered" threshold (more than 3 non-comment lines between library statements) on a file whose real imports are, in fact, perfectly grouped. Quantified across all 525 Python files flagged as scattered in the corpus: 155 (29.5%) have at least one spurious, non-import match of this kind; of those, 68 (13.0% of all 525 flagged files) would no longer be flagged as scattered at all once the spurious matches are excluded — pure false positives caused entirely by this mechanism (the remaining 87 files with a spurious match are still genuinely scattered even after excluding it). R showed essentially no equivalent problem in a 60-file sample (the one apparent candidate, on manual inspection, was a genuine conditional `require()` call, not a false positive — R's regex requires an opening parenthesis directly after the keyword, structurally harder to spuriously trigger than Python's bare whitespace-plus-word anchor). Fix: the Python pattern now requires the full import shape rather than just the leading keyword — a `from` line must also contain its own `import` keyword later on the same line (`^\s*from\s+[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_.]*\s+import\s`), and a bare `import` line must be followed by a comma-separated identifier list with an optional `as name` and nothing else (`^\s*import\s+[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_.]*(\s*,\s*[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_.]*)*(\s+as\s+\w+)?\s*$`) — verified against the docstring false-positive example above (now correctly unmatched) and against every real import shape found in the corpus sample, including multi-line `from x import (a, b, c)` continuations (matched on their opening line) and indented imports, with no loss of any real detection.

**Status of the fixes in this appendix.** All Metacheck fixes described in A.1 and A.3 (nine in total: #378, #379, #380, #383, both causes of #384, and the five `code_check` fixes from the systematic validation) have been committed to `scienceverse/metacheck`'s `repocheck_improvements` branch (pull request #385) and are covered by the package's automated test suite (463 tests passing at time of writing, 0 failures, 3 pre-existing skips unrelated to these changes). The sixth fix described above (the comparison script's missing-repository default) is not a Metacheck fix and has been committed instead to this project's own `code_data_preparation/03_recreate_cooper_columns.R`, in the `cooper_validation_metacheck` repository. The one defect identified but not yet fixed (`code_read()`'s crash on an empty file, A.2) and the two `code_file_refs()` limitations noted but not yet fixed (A.3) remain open. The further full corpus rerun incorporating the five A.3 fixes, planned when this appendix was first written, has since been performed (confirmed directly: the current corpus run's `code_check` output carries the `has_docstring` field A.3's docstring fix introduces, which cannot exist in a pre-fix run) — the numbers reported in "Results you get for free alongside Metacheck" above reflect that post-fix corpus, not the pre-fix state described earlier in this sentence's original drafting. This was a distinct item from the rerun described in Appendix A.5 below, which re-checked only the papers with a remaining disagreement (not the full corpus) and tested a different set of fixes (Zenodo reliability, repository-platform coverage, and rate-limit handling), not the five A.3 `code_check` fixes.

## A.4 A repository excluded from processing by file count

During the corpus rerun incorporating the A.3 fixes, one paper's data repository — Zenodo record 10.5281/zenodo.3971689, SAPFLUXNET (a global database of sap flow measurements: 202 datasets from 121 locations, sap flow and environmental time series for 2,714 individual plants) — was found to hold approximately 4,000 individual files. Downloading and, in particular, `data_check`'s per-file classification and full-content read of every one of those files (`data_check_head(..., n_rows = Inf)`, by design, since several of `data_check`'s validation checks need the complete dataset rather than a sample) took several hours and multiple gigabytes of memory for this single paper, out of 1,861 in the corpus, before the run was stopped.

This exposed a real gap in Metacheck: `download_repo_files()` already gates a repository outright by total byte size (`max_download_size`) or per-file byte size (`max_file_size`), but had no gate on file *count* — a repository holding thousands of individually small files was not caught by either existing cap. A new parameter, `max_files_per_repo` (`R/repo-download.R`, threaded through `data_check()` and `code_check()`), gates a repository by file count alone, using the same refusal/reporting mechanism as the existing size caps. This has been committed to the `repocheck_improvements` branch alongside a regression test, and the corpus rerun was configured with `max_files_per_repo = 1000`.

Under this cap, the SAPFLUXNET repository was refused outright in that run. The cap exists so that one exceptionally large repository cannot block or degrade processing of the other 1,860 papers in a corpus run. In the results reported in this manuscript, however, the repository was not refused: `data_check` lists all `r sum(structure_slim$paper_id == "10_1111_1365_2664_14383")` of its files, every one of them classified as data.

## A.5 A targeted rerun on every remaining disagreement, after further platform-detection and reliability fixes

After Appendix A.1–A.4's fixes and the resulting full corpus rerun, every remaining disagreement between Metacheck and Cooper et al.'s coding (991 rows across 989 papers, the same set individually adjudicated for the Empirical Comparison above) was re-checked a further time against Metacheck as it stood after seven more commits landed on `scienceverse/metacheck`'s `dev` branch: two fixing crashes and false negatives in Metacheck's Zenodo integration, three widening which repository *platforms* `repo_check` can locate a repository on at all (targeting "repository not detected," the single largest recurring disagreement cause identified in the original review), and two fixing a rate-limit reliability defect surfaced live during this rerun itself. Rather than reprocess the full 1,861-paper corpus, only the 989 papers with at least one open disagreement were rerun, one paper at a time (so that a single paper's slow host response could not block any other), reusing the shared on-disk repository-file cache from the original corpus run so that a repository already fetched and unchanged cost no new download.

**Zenodo reliability.** Two fixes addressed real crashes and false negatives in Metacheck's Zenodo integration, confirmed against Zenodo records already present in this corpus. `online()`, the function `repo_check` calls to confirm a host is reachable before querying it, treated a single transient DNS lookup miss as "Zenodo is offline" and abandoned that paper's entire Zenodo retrieval rather than retrying; it now retries. Separately, a JSON metadata field arriving as a length-zero value (an empty array) rather than `NULL` defeated the `%||%` operator used throughout Metacheck's metadata-extraction code (which only guards against `NULL`, not length-zero), producing a `data.frame()` "arguments imply differing number of rows" error that was silently swallowed inside a `tryCatch`, discarding the whole record; a new `%empty_or%` operator, applied everywhere the same gap existed (Dataverse, Dryad, DSpace7, Figshare, GitHub, GitLab, OSF, PsychArchives, and ReShare, not just Zenodo), closes this. A further, closely related pair of crashes was found and fixed the same way: a Zenodo record Metacheck could not read at all previously returned a `data.frame()` with only `zenodo_id`/`error` columns, so a paper whose every Zenodo record was unreadable produced a metadata table with no `doi`/`license` columns at all, which crashed `repo_check()`'s own Zenodo-metadata-extraction step for that paper the same "differing number of rows" way; and a `repo_url` arriving as a list column (rather than a plain character vector) could silently explode `data.frame(zenodo_url = <list>)` into one column per list element instead of the expected single column. Both are now guarded.

**Repository platform coverage.** Three commits substantially widened the set of hosts Metacheck's `repo_check` can locate a repository on at all, directly targeting the "repository not detected" cause responsible for the largest share of the original disagreement (the original review named DataSTORRE, DIGITAL.CSIC, AADC, SRA/GenBank, KNB, Neotoma, CIRAD Dataverse, and ForestPlots.net as example platforms with no backend at the time). Mendeley Data (detected via `10.17632/` DOIs and `data.mendeley.com` URLs, queried through the public, unauthenticated `data.mendeley.com/public-api/datasets/<id>` endpoint) and DataONE (a federation of independently-run repositories rather than one hosted service; four member nodes verified live and wired in — Arctic Data Center, KNB, Taiwan Forestry Research Institute, and the Smithsonian Tropical Data Portal, each mounting the same underlying REST API at a different base path) were added as new platforms entirely. Separately, Dataverse's recognised-installation list was expanded from 50 to 121 hosts, 16 institutional Figshare white-label front ends were added, and DSpace support was generalized from PsychArchives specifically to any host running the same legacy (≤6) API (5 more verified live) plus a new implementation covering 64 DSpace 7 installations (e.g. Cornell's eCommons, Georgia Tech's Digital Repository, ETH Zurich's Research Collection) — every one of these 121 + 16 + 5 + 64 hosts confirmed live via its own version/info endpoint before being added, not merely listed from a registry. A further, smaller fix excludes an R package's own source tree (`DESCRIPTION`/`NAMESPACE`/its `R/`/`man/`/`tests/` subdirectories) from a repository's data/code file listing, on the reasoning that reusable software infrastructure bundled alongside a study's own materials is not itself the study's data or analysis code and should not inflate `files_n`/`files_code` or appear in downstream reports.

**A reliability defect found live during this rerun.** While this rerun was in progress, a single paper stalled repeatedly at the same point across two separate attempts: `zip_peek()`'s HEAD request and its Range-request follow-up (`.http_range_tail()`, `R/zip-peek.R`), used to read a remote zip archive's file listing without downloading it, each independently hit Zenodo's rate limit and each, independently, paid the full announced wait for the host's confirmed reset — three consecutive confirmed-rate-limit waits back to back for what was, from Zenodo's own side, a single rate-limit window, since neither request had any way to know the other had already discovered and waited out the same limit. (The rate-limit-wait message itself was also, at the same time, made to name the specific host responsible — Zenodo, Dryad, GitHub, or GitLab, the only hosts that expose a machine-readable reset time — rather than reporting only "the host's own reset," a smaller, secondary fix made in the course of diagnosing this one.) Fix: a session-scoped record of the last confirmed rate-limit reset per host, written the first time any request discovers one and consulted by every subsequent request to that host before it is even sent, so a host already known to be rate-limited waits out only the genuinely remaining time once, rather than every independent request rediscovering the identical window from a fresh 429. Verified with new regression tests covering the record/lookup logic directly (round-tripping a wait, keeping the later of two recorded resets, clearing an expired window, and the pre-flight wait actually sleeping the correct duration) and confirmed live: the same paper that previously stalled for over 40 minutes across three stacked waits resolved in roughly 3 minutes with zero confirmed-rate-limit waits after the fix, the remaining time attributable to Zenodo's own server-side response latency for that specific record (confirmed independently: a single isolated request to the same record, made outside Metacheck entirely, itself took 30 seconds and returned a 504 on a second attempt).

**Results of the rerun.** Across the 1,532 individual construct-level disagreements re-checked (989 papers × up to 7 constructs each, matching however many constructs a given paper had originally disagreed on), 76.8% (1,176 of 1,532) are now resolved — Metacheck's fresh result agrees with Cooper et al.'s original human coding where it did not before — with 348 still disagreeing and 1 now returning a value that could not be classified as agreeing or disagreeing (`data_license`, a repository whose licence field this rerun could not read for reasons not yet diagnosed). By construct: `any_readme` 548/625 resolved (87.7%), `data_availability` 339/424 (80.0%), `code_archived` 252/360 (70.0%), `data_archive` 12/56 (21.4%, evaluated by set membership — a paper's platform coded by Cooper now appearing among Metacheck's own, possibly multi-platform, detected set, since a paper can genuinely link more than one repository), `data_license` 16/57 (28.1%), `data_download` 9/9 (100%), and `code_download` 0/1 (the sole remaining `code_download` disagreement in this corpus). The comparatively modest improvement in `data_archive` and `data_license` is consistent with the original review's own finding that these two constructs' disagreement was, unlike `data_availability`/`code_archived`/`any_readme`, not dominated by the repository-detection cause these fixes targeted (`data_license`'s largest cause was cases where Metacheck was already right and Cooper's own coding had missed a real licence field) — a fix aimed at finding more repositories naturally does less for a construct whose disagreement was rarely about a missing repository in the first place. This rerun's full row-level detail (every paper, every re-checked construct, the value before and after, and whether it resolved) is recorded in `cooper_validation_metacheck/manuscript/data/rerun_disagreements_comparison.csv`, produced by `rerun_disagreements.R`; the underlying per-paper `repo_check`/`data_check`/`code_check` results are cached per paper in `data/rerun_batches/` for inspection or a further rerun without recomputing what has not changed.

**Checking the rest of the corpus for regressions.** This rerun was scoped to the 989 previously-disagreeing papers only — a deliberate choice at the time, to get a fast answer to "did these fixes help" without the cost of a full 1,861-paper rerun (see the rerun's own header comment for the reasoning). That scoping left one real question open: none of these seven fixes were written to only affect a disagreeing paper, so it remained possible that a fix which resolved one paper's disagreement had, in a different paper that already agreed with Cooper et al., turned a correct result into an incorrect one — most plausibly the R-package-source-tree exclusion (if a paper's own analysis code happens to be organised as an R package) or the expanded Dataverse/Figshare/DSpace/Mendeley/DataONE host recognition (a newly-recognised host matching something that should not have counted). This was checked directly: the remaining 868 papers (every paper not in the 989-paper disagreement set) were also rerun, using the identical per-paper, resumable approach, and the full corpus's `cooper_vs_recreated.RData`/disagreement worklist were then rebuilt from the combined result (all 1,861 papers) rather than just the 989. At the level of aggregate agreement rates, this full-corpus check was reassuring: the three constructs this comparison's own disagreement was concentrated in — `data_availability`, `code_archived`, `any_readme` — all showed a higher, not lower, agreement rate once the previously-agreeing papers were included, and `data_download`/`code_download` (both already above 99%) moved by less than a percentage point in either direction. But an aggregate rate rising is consistent with a handful of individual papers having genuinely regressed, provided enough *other* papers improved to more than offset them — and that is exactly what the case-by-case review below found.

**A confirmed regression, found and fixed within this same cycle.** The suspicion named above turned out to be correct: the R-package-source-tree exclusion did break papers it should not have touched. The exclusion was written to detect an R package's fingerprint (a `DESCRIPTION` and `NAMESPACE` file in the same folder) and drop that folder's contents — the package's `R/`, `man/`, `tests/`, `vignettes/`, `data/`, `inst/`, and `src/` subdirectories — from a repository's file listing entirely, on the reasoning that a bundled, reusable software dependency is not itself a study's data or analysis code. That reasoning holds when the package is a genuine dependency vendored alongside a study's own files, but it does not hold when the paper's *own* contribution — its data, its analysis code, or both — is itself packaged and distributed as an installable R package, a common practice in ecological/evolutionary methods work. In that case the exclusion strips the paper's own materials, leaving nothing behind: `repo_check`'s listing for the affected repository showed only packaging scaffolding (`.Rbuildignore`, `.gitignore`, `NEWS.md`, `README.md`, `cran-comments.md`, a bare `.Rproj` file), with the package's real `R/` source — and, for packages that bundle their own example or study data under `data/`, the actual dataset — entirely absent.

A corpus-wide scan for this exact symptom (a repository whose only surviving files, after the exclusion ran, were scaffolding, with zero files classified as data or code) surfaced candidates across the full 1,861-paper corpus, each individually verified against the repository's real GitHub listing (via `gh api`) or Dryad/Zenodo record before being counted: 16 confirmed true instances (`RevGadgets`, `BaBA`, `m2b`, `RRPP`, `actel`, `scampr`, `MINOTAUR`, `LadderFuelsR`, `biomonitoR`, `EcoEnsemble`, `fossilsim`, `frair`, `tRophicPosition`, `sabinaNSDM`, `bef`, and `phylomice`), plus several candidates from the same scan that turned out to be unrelated causes once checked directly (a repository with no `DESCRIPTION`/`NAMESPACE` at all, and several Dryad/Zenodo-hosted papers whose `code_archived` disagreement traced to an unconnected, pre-existing detection gap — code cited in a journal's own Supporting Information, or a repository never located by `repo_check` at all). Two confirmed cases (`BaBA`, a GitHub-hosted barrier-behaviour-analysis package whose `data/` folder holds the actual tracked-animal datasets for its own paper, and `MGDrivE`, a general-purpose mosquito gene-drive simulation package vendored inside a study-specific fork) between them illustrated the structural distinction the fix needed to draw: `BaBA`'s package sits at its repository's root with nothing else present — the package *is* the deposit, so nothing should be excluded — while `MGDrivE`'s vendored copy is nested one level deep inside the fork, with the study's own `Examples/` scripts and data sitting as real, undisputed siblings at the repository root.

The corrected rule preserves the original exclusion's logic for a nested package (still always excluded, on the assumption that a nested package always has the study's own files beside it; the `good` package, which sits alone in a subfolder, shows that this can fail, scienceverse/metacheck#505) but adds one check for a package detected at a repository's *root*: before excluding it, check whether anything outside the package folder classifies as real data or code, using `data_classify_files()` — the same rules-based classifier `data_check` itself uses elsewhere in the pipeline, rather than a separate, bespoke list of what counts as "real content." If nothing does, the package is not excluded at all, since there is no "outside" for the study's own materials to live in. One implementation detail required a second pass: an RStudio project marker file (`*.Rproj`) classifies as `"code"` under `data_classify_files()` purely by its file extension, which would have wrongly counted as "real content survives" for every package that ships one (nearly all of them) — an RStudio project file is packaging configuration, not an analysis script, so it is excluded from this specific check. The fix was verified against two new regression tests (a root-level package with nothing else present, confirming it is no longer excluded, and a nested vendored package alongside real sibling content, confirming the vendored files are still excluded while the sibling content survives) alongside the existing test suite, then reapplied to the 38 papers the corpus-wide scan had flagged.

Reapplying the corrected exclusion resolved 11 of the 16 confirmed cases outright. The remaining 5 continued to show `code_archived` disagreement. An earlier version of this manuscript attributed these to the package's `R/` directory never having been downloaded; a later direct check showed that explanation was wrong. The file listing was complete, but the corrected rule itself misfired: the rule made an exception for RStudio project files, as described above, but not for continuous-integration configuration files at the repository root (such as `.travis.yml` and `codecov.yml`), which are classified as code by their extension. The rule therefore concluded that real code survived outside the package and kept excluding the package's own source files. This was confirmed in detail for `biomonitoR` (238 files retrieved, 229 of them excluded) and reported as scienceverse/metacheck#469. Metacheck 0.3.3.3 fixed it by making the same exception for continuous-integration files; after a rerun of the affected papers with Metacheck 0.3.3.11, `r n_rpkg16_resolved` of the 16 have their code found. Two of the 16, `phylomice` and `morton` — cases surfaced by the same corpus-wide scan but outside the original 13-paper set found during the initial regression check — resolved to, respectively, `METACHECK_RIGHT` (`phylomice`'s six R source files are a genuine methods contribution the paper's own text never explicitly claims as "archived code," but which Metacheck is nonetheless correct to report) and `COOPER_RIGHT` (`morton`'s 37 R source files are unambiguously this paper's own phylogenetic-analysis code, which Cooper et al.'s coders had missed).

## A.6 A systematic platform-coverage audit, three further metacheck fixes, and a complete categorization of every remaining repository-detection disagreement

A sixth round of work started from a single case the previous rounds had not caught: a paper citing a Dataverse installation (`borealisdata.ca`, Borealis, the Canadian national repository) under a DOI prefix Appendix A.5's Dataverse allowlist did not recognise. Tracing why surfaced a systemic problem in how that allowlist had been built, and prompted a full re-audit of every remaining "repository not detected" disagreement in the corpus rather than a single-paper patch.

**A systemic under-sampling bug in the Dataverse DOI-prefix allowlist.** Appendix A.5's per-host Dataverse DOI-prefix allowlist (`.dataverse_doi_prefix_hosts()`) was originally built by sampling the first 25 DOIs DataCite's search API returned for each host — a sample, not a census. This badly under-counted any host with more than 25 real DOIs registered, which turned out to be the majority of the 121 known hosts; `borealisdata.ca` alone has minted DOIs under six distinct prefixes, of which the original allowlist recorded only one. Rebuilding the allowlist using DataCite's facet aggregation (`disable-facets=false` on its `/dois` search, which returns every distinct prefix in use for a host, with its real count, in one request rather than a sample) found 100 distinct prefixes across the same 87 hosts, not 87 — including a second Harvard Dataverse prefix (`10.26300`, alongside the dominant `10.7910`) that the original sample had also missed. Verified live before and after: the DOI that surfaced this bug (`10.7939/DVN/M6Q2PE`, Borealis) now resolves correctly, and the second Harvard prefix now resolves to `dataverse.harvard.edu`. This was reported and merged upstream as scienceverse/metacheck#410.

**Two further platform-coverage gaps found and fixed the same way.** `.figshare_id()` did not recognise a Figshare article URL with no resource-type segment (`figshare.com/articles/<slug>/<id>`, as opposed to `figshare.com/articles/dataset/<slug>/<id>`) — an older, still-current URL shape (confirmed live against a real corpus citation) that `figshare_links()` already detected as a Figshare link but could not resolve to a usable article id, so `repo_check` never actually queried it (scienceverse/metacheck#412). Separately, `dataone_links()` had no entry for `data.piscoweb.org` (PISCO, a UC Santa Barbara-run DataONE member node), and `.dataone_pid()`'s bare-DOI regex could not handle a DOI suffix containing a further slash — PISCO's own DOI shape (`10.6085/AA/<id>`) — so this platform's citations, while real DataONE member-node DOIs, were invisible end to end. Both fixed and merged as scienceverse/metacheck#414, which also added 29 further institutional Figshare instances (28 found by searching DataCite's client registry for "figshare" in the client name, plus Monash University's `bridges.monash.edu`, found separately since its DataCite client is registered under the institution's own name) — each confirmed live, the same way as every host already in `.figshare_vanity_hosts()`, to answer Figshare's own single-page-app shell rather than a real API response, and each institutional DOI prefix confirmed live to resolve to that exact host before being added.

**Two matching bugs in this project's own comparison code, not in Metacheck.** `03_recreate_cooper_columns.R`'s `.repo_url_platform()` — the function that labels which platform `mc_data_archive` reports for a paper — had a Dryad branch that only matched the single most common DOI prefix (`10.5061`), and a Figshare branch that only matched the literal `figshare.com`/`10.6084` domain and prefix, missing every one of the alternate Dryad prefixes and institutional Figshare instances Metacheck itself already recognised after the fixes above. The practical effect was a paper whose repository *was* now correctly found and retrieved still showing a `data_archive` disagreement, because the label fell through to the generic "Other repo/database" instead of naming the real platform. Both branches were rewritten to read directly from Metacheck's own `.dryad_doi_prefixes()`/`.figshare_vanity_hosts()`/`.figshare_doi_prefix_hosts()` rather than duplicating either list by hand, so this classification cannot drift out of sync with what Metacheck itself recognises again.

**Reprocessing every paper these fixes could plausibly affect.** Rather than assume the fixes above were the only remaining cause of repository-detection disagreement, every "repository not detected" comment still open in the worklist (351 individual (paper, column) disagreements across 233 papers, after excluding platforms already confirmed unsupported for an unrelated reason) was checked again: first narrowed locally, with no network calls, to the papers whose cited DOI prefix genuinely matched one of the platforms just fixed (27 candidates, after excluding two DOI prefixes that coincidentally collide with an unrelated platform's registered prefix in DataCite's own data — `10.6084`, Figshare's own prefix, and `10.17617`, Edmond's — neither of which any fix above touched), then live-verified one at a time. Of those 27, 13 were genuinely resolved by the fixes above; the remaining 14 were not — some detect the citation correctly but the dataset is embargoed or restricted at the source (confirmed via the repository's own API returning an explicit "cannot be viewed" message, not a Metacheck-side failure), and a few still do not detect the citation at all, for reasons unrelated to any fix in this round. A further, separately-run check across every remaining "never located" comment surfaced one exact repeat of Appendix A.1's original zip-peek limitation on a much larger scale (24 papers whose Zenodo/Figshare/Dataverse archive was never successfully peeked during an earlier corpus build, confirmed live, unmodified, to peek correctly today — a stale corpus row in every one of the 24, not a code defect). A further paper, initially suspected to be a second such stale row (its earlier 4TU fetch crash was already fixed in Appendix A.1 and appeared simply never rerun since), was checked directly against `rerun_disagreements_comparison.csv`'s own before/after values and found to still disagree after being rerun — the 4TU fetch failure was not, in fact, resolved. A later, more thorough recheck (Appendix A.9) traced the actual cause: 4TU is a genuinely supported platform, but its DOI-embedded identifier does not match the numeric article ID 4TU's own API requires, a distinct defect from the one Appendix A.1 fixed, so the paper was counted as `SUPPORTED_PLATFORM_BUG`, not `UNSUPPORTED_REPO`, in Appendix A.9's categorization. Since the rerun with Metacheck 0.3.3.11 (17 October 2026), Metacheck lists this 4TU record (7 files, 5 of them data) and finds the paper's data. All resolved candidates from this round were rerun end to end (`repo_check`, `data_check`, `code_check`) and patched into the corpus; none of this round's rerunning touched a paper outside the specific set each check identified, so no regression check across the unaffected remainder of the corpus was needed the way Appendix A.5's broader platform-coverage changes required.

## A.7 A full-corpus `reproducibility_check` run: method, outputs, reasons for non-reproducibility, and suggested improvements to Metacheck

A seventh round of work ran Metacheck's `reproducibility_check` module — a module distinct from `repo_check`/`data_check`/`code_check` (the three modules the rest of this manuscript is about) in that it does not merely detect and classify a paper's shared data and code, but actually **executes** the paper's own downloaded code against the paper's own shared data, inside an isolated sandbox, and checks whether the statistical results the code produces match what the paper itself reports in its text. This appendix documents the method, the files this run produced, a full breakdown of why papers were and were not reproducible, two Metacheck defects this run surfaced (both reported upstream, one fixed on `dev` and used to produce the final result for the one paper it had stopped), and a set of concrete suggestions for further improving `reproducibility_check` itself.

### A.7.1 Method

`reproducibility_check` was run with `code/run_metacheck.R` on the 435 papers in which an earlier module run had found runnable R or Python code (the subset of the 1,861-paper corpus with code to execute; the other 1,426 papers have no code for the module to run, and are not discussed further in this section). For each paper, the module: (1) reuses `code_check`'s dependency extraction and `psychds_check`'s path-rewrite plan to materialise a throwaway copy of the paper's own Psych-DS-layout data and code; (2) installs the paper's declared package dependencies (CRAN, GitHub, Bioconductor, or URL sources) into a throwaway library inside a Docker container, starting from a pre-built image (`ghcr.io/scienceverse/metacheck_r_large` for R, `ghcr.io/scienceverse/metacheck_py_large` for Python) in which the most common packages found across a prior corpus scan are already installed, so most papers skip most of the install step; (3) runs each of the paper's scripts, in an automatically-derived dependency order, each in its own Docker container, with the filesystem read-only outside the materialised sandbox — a genuine containment boundary for running downloaded, unvetted third-party code; and (4) extracts any statistical output the executed scripts printed to the console and compares it against the paper's own reported results (`match_reported_output()`), recording how many of the paper's own reported test statistics the executed code actually reproduced.

The run used Metacheck commit `f6aec07c` (version 0.4.3.6), three papers at a time (`--workers 3`), each container limited to 4 GB of memory and a share of 6.6 processors, a 3,000-second time limit per script and 3,600 seconds for all of a paper's scripts together, a 1,200-second limit on installing a paper's packages, a 1,000 MB limit on any single file downloaded, and internet access allowed during execution (so a script that fetches a file over the network could still run, at the cost that what it downloaded may differ from what the authors had). The scripts could use the internet up to 1,000 MB per file and 2,000 MB for all of a paper's scripts together. Each paper's complete result was written to its own file the moment that paper finished, so a run interrupted partway through — which happened several times, because the drive holding the sandbox and the downloaded data repeatedly filled — did not lose the papers that had already completed; restarting skipped every paper with a saved result and ran only those still outstanding.

Two of the 435 papers were run on a different Docker image or a different Metacheck version than the other 433, for reasons given in A.7.5, and each paper's result records which run and which commit produced it (`run_info$paper_runs`): 58 papers whose code needed a package that would not compile for lack of a system header file were run again on an image with those headers added (`ghcr.io/scienceverse/metacheck_r_large:headers-2026-11-07`), and one paper (10.1111/2041-210X.13928) whose reproducibility check the main version could not complete at all was run on the `dev` branch (commit with the fix for that defect, version 0.4.3.13). The matching of reported results to the code's output (step 4 above) was computed afterwards from the saved console output with `code/match_reported_results.R`, run once with the `dev` version for every paper, without running any script again.

### A.7.2 Outputs stored

The run wrote one `.rds` file per paper, each holding that paper's complete result across every module, into a run folder on the drive used for the run. `code/splice_reproducibility.R` combined the main run with the two follow-up runs named above into `data/metacheck_results.rds`, the single file every number in this manuscript is computed from; it records, for each paper, which of the three runs and which Metacheck commit produced its reproducibility result. Each paper's own result carries the per-script table (one row per script attempted, with its `outcome`, the one-word `reason` the module assigned a script that did not run through, the file paths the module rewrote, the `setwd()` calls it removed, and the packages it declared and installed) and the per-paper summary row (`repro_code_n`, the count of scripts that were run as analyses, the per-reason failure counts, and the reported-versus-reproduced statistic counts).

### A.7.3 Scope: which papers had code to check at all

```{r}
#| label: a7-reproducibility-load

# Every number in A.7.3-A.7.4 is computed here from the targets
# reproducibility_results and reproducibility_detail (code/R/metacheck_results.R),
# on the same counting scheme as the body of the manuscript: a script is counted
# only if the module ran it as an analysis of its own (the excluded outcomes below
# are the module's own, matching Metacheck's .repro_run_counts()).
targets::tar_load(reproducibility_results, store = "_targets")
targets::tar_load(reproducibility_detail, store = "_targets")
rp_tab_all <- reproducibility_results$table
rp_st <- reproducibility_results$summary_table
rp_d <- reproducibility_detail
fmt <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",")
pct_of <- function(x, n) sprintf("%.1f", 100 * x / n)

rp_n_papers <- nrow(rp_st)
rp_code_bearing <- rp_st$paper_id[!is.na(rp_st$repro_code_n) & rp_st$repro_code_n > 0]
rp_n_cb <- length(rp_code_bearing)
rp_n_none <- sum(rp_st$repro_code_n %in% 0)

# Outcomes that are not a standalone analysis script, counted and named apart.
rp_excluded <- c("run_by_source", "run_by_import", "jags_model", "not_r_content",
                 "defines_functions", "not_analysis", "docker_failed", "not_downloaded")
rp_nx <- function(o) sum(rp_tab_all$outcome %in% o)
rp_n_source <- rp_nx(c("run_by_source", "run_by_import"))
rp_n_defines <- rp_nx("defines_functions")
rp_n_jags <- rp_nx("jags_model")
rp_n_not_analysis <- rp_nx("not_analysis")
rp_n_not_r_content <- rp_nx("not_r_content")
rp_n_not_downloaded <- rp_nx("not_downloaded")

rp_tab <- rp_tab_all[!rp_tab_all$outcome %in% rp_excluded & !is.na(rp_tab_all$outcome), ]
rp_n_scripts <- nrow(rp_tab)
rp_ext <- tolower(tools::file_ext(rp_tab$file_name))
rp_n_py_scripts <- sum(rp_ext %in% c("py", "ipynb"))
rp_out <- function(o) sum(rp_tab$outcome %in% o)
rp_n_ok <- sum(rp_tab$outcome == "ran_ok")

rp_by_paper <- split(rp_tab$outcome == "ran_ok", rp_tab$paper_id)
rp_n_all_ok <- sum(vapply(rp_by_paper, all, logical(1)))
rp_n_none_ok <- sum(!vapply(rp_by_paper, any, logical(1)))
rp_n_mixed <- length(rp_by_paper) - rp_n_all_ok - rp_n_none_ok
rp_n_ran_ok_papers <- sum(vapply(rp_by_paper, any, logical(1)))

# The module's one-word reason for each counted script that did not run through.
rp_reason <- rp_tab$reason
rp_reason[rp_tab$outcome == "ran_ok"] <- NA_character_
rp_n_failed <- sum(!is.na(rp_reason))
rp_n_failed_papers <- length(unique(rp_tab$paper_id[!is.na(rp_reason)]))
rp_rn <- function(r) sum(rp_reason %in% r)
rp_rn_papers <- function(r) length(unique(rp_tab$paper_id[rp_reason %in% r]))

# Install failures: one row per paper and package, from the module's own records,
# each carrying a classified category and reason.
rp_failed <- rp_d$per_paper_failed_deps
rp_n_failed_records <- nrow(rp_failed)
rp_n_failed_pkg_papers <- length(unique(rp_failed$paper_id))
rp_n_failed_pkgs <- length(unique(rp_failed$package))
rp_cat <- function(c) sum(rp_failed$category %in% c)
rp_fz <- rp_d$pkg_counts_failed_and_zero_ok
rp_n_fz_papers <- length(rp_d$failed_and_zero_ok_papers)
rp_fz_n <- function(p) { n <- rp_fz$n_papers_failed[rp_fz$package == p]; if (length(n)) n else 0L }
rp_spatial <- c("sf", "rgdal", "rgeos", "maptools", "stars", "ggspatial", "mapview", "tmap",
                "gdalUtils", "nngeo", "spatial.tools")
rp_n_spatial_records <- sum(rp_failed$package %in% rp_spatial)

rp_m <- rp_d$all_matches
rp_bp <- rp_d$by_paper_match
rp_n_match_papers <- nrow(rp_bp)
rp_n_match_rows <- nrow(rp_m)
rp_n_matched <- sum(rp_m$found %in% TRUE)
rp_n_all_matched <- sum(rp_bp$prop_matched == 1)
rp_n_none_matched <- sum(rp_bp$prop_matched == 0)
rp_n_some_matched <- rp_n_match_papers - rp_n_all_matched - rp_n_none_matched
rp_n_full <- sum(rp_m$confidence[rp_m$found %in% TRUE] %in% "full")
rp_n_partial <- sum(rp_m$confidence[rp_m$found %in% TRUE] %in% "partial")
rp_n_unmatched <- sum(!rp_m$found %in% TRUE)
rp_n_plausible <- sum(rp_m$plausible_split[!rp_m$found %in% TRUE] %in% TRUE)
```

Of the `r fmt(rp_n_papers)` papers in the corpus, `r rp_n_cb` (`r pct_of(rp_n_cb, rp_n_papers)`%) had at least one runnable code file for `reproducibility_check` to attempt (`repro_code_n > 0`); `r fmt(rp_n_none)` (`r pct_of(rp_n_none, rp_n_papers)`%) had none, and are not further discussed in this section, since there is nothing for the module to execute — this is the same "does the paper share any code" question `code_check`/`repo_check` already answer elsewhere in this manuscript, not a new finding. The reproducibility run therefore covered these `r rp_n_cb` code-bearing papers.

**Note on this count.** Every number in this section is computed on the same scheme as the body of the manuscript: a file is counted among the scripts that were run only if the module ran it as an analysis of its own. The files it did not (a file run by another through `source()` or an import, a file that only defines functions, a JAGS or BUGS model file, a file that is not code in a language the module runs, and a file not downloaded) are counted and named apart. The comparison of reported results with the code's output was computed afterwards from the saved output, without running any script again.

### A.7.4 Reasons for non-reproducibility: a full breakdown

Across the `r rp_n_cb` code-bearing papers, `r fmt(rp_n_scripts)` scripts were run as analyses, `r fmt(rp_n_py_scripts)` of them Python (`.py` or `.ipynb`) and the rest R. Not every code file is such a script: a further `r fmt(rp_n_source)` files are run by another script through `source()` or an import and have no result of their own, `r rp_n_defines` only define functions, `r rp_n_jags` are JAGS or BUGS model files, `r rp_n_not_r_content` are not code in a language the module runs, and `r rp_n_not_downloaded` needed a data file too large to download; these are counted apart and are not included below. Of the `r fmt(rp_n_scripts)` scripts that were run, `r fmt(rp_n_ok)` (`r pct_of(rp_n_ok, rp_n_scripts)`%) ran without an error. Their outcomes:

| Outcome | Count | % of `r fmt(rp_n_scripts)` |
|---|---|---|
| `ran_ok` (ran without an error) | `r fmt(rp_out("ran_ok"))` | `r pct_of(rp_out("ran_ok"), rp_n_scripts)`% |
| `errored` (ran, but raised an error) | `r fmt(rp_out("errored"))` | `r pct_of(rp_out("errored"), rp_n_scripts)`% |
| `dependency_unavailable` (a package it needs could not be installed, so it was not run) | `r fmt(rp_out("dependency_unavailable"))` | `r pct_of(rp_out("dependency_unavailable"), rp_n_scripts)`% |
| `needs_a_person` (the code asks a person to choose a file, so it cannot run unattended) | `r fmt(rp_out("needs_a_person"))` | `r pct_of(rp_out("needs_a_person"), rp_n_scripts)`% |
| `skipped_time_limit` (not started, because the paper's time had run out) | `r fmt(rp_out("skipped_time_limit"))` | `r pct_of(rp_out("skipped_time_limit"), rp_n_scripts)`% |
| `not_parsed` (the file is not valid syntax in its language) | `r fmt(rp_out("not_parsed"))` | `r pct_of(rp_out("not_parsed"), rp_n_scripts)`% |
| `timed_out` (still running at the 3,000-second cutoff) | `r fmt(rp_out("timed_out"))` | `r pct_of(rp_out("timed_out"), rp_n_scripts)`% |
| `download_too_large` (a file it needs was over the download limit) | `r fmt(rp_out("download_too_large"))` | `r pct_of(rp_out("download_too_large"), rp_n_scripts)`% |
| `out_of_memory` (stopped by the memory limit) | `r fmt(rp_out("out_of_memory"))` | `r pct_of(rp_out("out_of_memory"), rp_n_scripts)`% |
| `needs_internet` (needs network access the sandbox blocks for that host) | `r fmt(rp_out("needs_internet"))` | `r pct_of(rp_out("needs_internet"), rp_n_scripts)`% |

**At the paper level**, only `r rp_n_all_ok` of the `r rp_n_cb` code-bearing papers (`r pct_of(rp_n_all_ok, rp_n_cb)`%) had *every one* of their scripts run without error; `r rp_n_none_ok` (`r pct_of(rp_n_none_ok, rp_n_cb)`%) had *zero* scripts run successfully at all; the remaining `r rp_n_mixed` (`r pct_of(rp_n_mixed, rp_n_cb)`%) had a mix of successful and failed scripts within the same paper.

**Why the `r fmt(rp_n_failed)` scripts that did not run through failed.** The module records a one-word reason for each; the same reasons are reported, with their counts, in the body of the manuscript. The largest is a file the script needs that was not found (`r rp_rn("file")` scripts, in `r rp_rn_papers("file")` papers): the authors did not archive it, it is produced by an earlier step that is not archived, or the name in the code could not be matched to a file in the deposit. Next is a catch-all for an error that fits none of the named reasons (`r rp_rn("other")`), then a package that could not be installed (`r rp_rn("package")`), code that asks a person to choose a file (`r rp_rn("interactive")`), the time limit (`r rp_rn("time")`), an object or function that is not defined (`r rp_rn("undefined")`, the signature of a script meant to run as one step of a larger pipeline), a file that is not valid code (`r rp_rn("syntax")`), a difference in the software environment (`r rp_rn("environment")`), a download too large (`r rp_rn("download")`), and a script that needs the internet (`r rp_rn("internet")`).

Two directly observed patterns are worth naming, because both argue the code was never meant to run unattended: a script that calls `file.choose()` to open an interactive file-picker, which cannot work in a headless container (the module records these as `needs_a_person`), and a script that starts a blocking viewer such as `rstanarm::launch_shinystan()`, which waits for a browser connection that never arrives and is stopped only by the time limit.
