**Dependency installation.** Before running a paper's code, Metacheck installs the R or Python packages that code declares it needs, from a Docker image in which the most common packages are already present. Across the `r rp_n_cb` papers, `r fmt(rp_n_failed_records)` package installs failed, in `r rp_n_failed_pkg_papers` papers, naming `r rp_n_failed_pkgs` distinct packages (most failing in a single paper). The module records, for each, a classified category: the largest group is a package found on neither CRAN nor Bioconductor and not anywhere else the module looks, because the code does not say where it comes from; the next are a package that fails to compile, and a package no longer available on CRAN for the version of R the run used. The packages that needed a system development library the image did not contain (the GDAL/GEOS files behind `rgdal`, `rgeos` and `gdalUtils`, and the compression headers behind several Bioconductor packages) are not in these counts, because the 58-paper rerun on the image with those headers added (A.7.5) installed them; what remains is the set no added header could fix.

In `r rp_n_fz_papers` papers, a package failed to install and no script of the paper ran successfully — the subset where a failed install is most clearly the reason the code did not run. For these, giving the Docker install backend the CRAN Archive retry the other backend already has (A.7.6) could recover a share of the packages that were removed from CRAN but still have a version in the Archive.

**Result matching: did the code's own output match what the paper reports?** Beyond running a paper's code, `reproducibility_check` extracts each statistical result the paper's own text reports (a *t*-test, a correlation, a regression coefficient) and checks whether that value appears in what the executed code printed (`match_reported_output()`). This is the closest the run comes to asking not just "does the code run" but "does running it get the paper's own numbers." It also reads the result tables inside a self-reproducible `.jasp`/`.omv`/`.spv` file (JASP, jamovi, or SPSS Viewer), which carry data and analysis together and need no code execution, and feeds them into the same step.

`r rp_n_match_papers` papers had at least one statistical result the module could both extract from the paper's text and attempt to match against the code's output; across those papers, `r fmt(rp_n_match_rows)` reported statistics were checked, of which `r rp_n_matched` (`r pct_of(rp_n_matched, rp_n_match_rows)`%) were matched. At the paper level, `r rp_n_all_matched` of the `r rp_n_match_papers` papers (`r pct_of(rp_n_all_matched, rp_n_match_papers)`%) had the code reproduce *every* reported result checked, `r rp_n_none_matched` (`r pct_of(rp_n_none_matched, rp_n_match_papers)`%) reproduced *none*, and the remaining `r rp_n_some_matched` (`r pct_of(rp_n_some_matched, rp_n_match_papers)`%) reproduced some but not all. This is best read together with the outcome breakdown above rather than as a claim about the research: a script has to run to completion and print a value before that value can be compared to the text at all, and only `r pct_of(rp_n_ok, rp_n_scripts)`% of scripts, and `r pct_of(rp_n_all_ok, rp_n_cb)`% of papers in full, cleared that first bar.

The matching step draws one further distinction worth keeping. Of the `r rp_n_matched` matched values, `r rp_n_full` (`r pct_of(rp_n_full, rp_n_matched)`%) matched at full confidence (every component of the reported test matched together) and `r rp_n_partial` (`r pct_of(rp_n_partial, rp_n_matched)`%) only partially; when the code did reproduce a value, it usually reproduced it completely. And of the `r fmt(rp_n_unmatched)` values not matched, `r rp_n_plausible` were nonetheless traced to a real quantity the code computed under a different grouping than the paper's text suggested — a materially less serious finding than a value the code never produced at all.

**A note on scope and what this section does not claim.** These numbers describe whether a paper's own downloaded code, as shared, ran and reproduced its own reported results in this execution environment, with its pre-installed package set, its 3,000-second per-script budget, and the internet available during execution. A script failing here is not evidence the paper's research is wrong, or even that the code never worked — it may never have been meant to run outside the authors' own machine, as the `file.choose()` and "designed as an interactive pipeline" patterns above show directly. A full per-paper review of why each failed script failed, in the style of Appendix A.1–A.6's disagreement-by-disagreement review, is listed as a further step in A.7.6 rather than attempted here.

### A.7.5 Infrastructure failures, found and fixed during this run

Running `reproducibility_check` on all 435 code-bearing papers surfaced two defects in Metacheck itself — neither related to a paper's own code or data — and two operational problems with the run's own environment that required part of the corpus to be run again. Both defects were filed as issues against `scienceverse/metacheck`.

**scienceverse/metacheck#597 — a file name is not escaped before it is used as a regular expression, which stops the module for a paper.** When the module rewrites a script's file paths to point at the downloaded files, it builds a search pattern from each file name, but the code that was meant to escape characters with a special meaning in a regular expression used a form that, without Perl mode, escaped nothing. A file name containing a Windows path with a backslash followed by a letter (for example `\P` or `\s`) therefore produced an invalid regular expression, which stopped the whole reproducibility check for that paper before any script was run. One paper in this corpus hit it (10.1111/2041-210X.13928, whose code names the path `D:\AviaNZ\Sound_Files\...`). The defect was fixed on the `dev` branch (the four affected call sites now use the escape function that works), and this one paper was run again on that version (0.4.3.13) to produce its reproducibility result, which is the result reported here for it. **Confirmed fixed.**

**scienceverse/metacheck#598 — an install address in a commented-out line is used instead of CRAN.** For one paper (10.1111/1365-2435.13410), the module installed a package from a web address that appears only inside a commented-out line of the paper's own code, rather than from CRAN; the address was dead, so the install failed. The defect is that the dependency extractor reads an install address out of a line the R interpreter would never run. This affects which source a package is installed from, not whether the module runs, so it did not stop any paper. **Filed, open.**

**Fifty-eight papers run again on an image with system header files.** The pre-built R image used for the main run did not contain the C and C++ header files that some packages need in order to compile from source (for example `zlib.h`, needed by several Bioconductor packages, and the GDAL/GEOS development files needed by the spatial packages `rgdal`, `rgeos` and `gdalUtils`). A package that needs such a header could not install, so the scripts that load it could not run. After the main run, the project built an image with these development files added, confirmed in it the packages that the main run could not install now did, and ran again, on that image, the 58 papers whose code needed one of those packages. Every package the new image was meant to provide then installed; the packages that still failed are ones no added header could fix (a package with no findable source, one removed from CRAN, or one that fails to compile for an unrelated reason). Each of these 58 papers' reproducibility result in the combined output is the result from this second run, recorded as such in `run_info$paper_runs`.

**Repeated interruptions from the run drive filling.** The drive holding the sandbox, the downloaded repositories and Docker's own data repeatedly ran low on free space during the run, because a paper that was stopped — by its time limit, by a stall, or by the low-space guard itself — left its unpacked copy of the deposit behind, and these accumulated across the run. The run has a built-in guard that starts no new paper below 10 GB of free space and stops the running papers below 5 GB, so each time the drive filled the run stopped itself rather than failing in some uncontrolled way; it was restarted after the leftover copies were deleted, and because each paper's result is saved the moment it finishes, every restart skipped the papers already done and ran only those outstanding. This is a property of the environment the run was carried out in, not of Metacheck or of any paper's code, but it is the reason the run was completed in several stretches rather than one.

### A.7.6 Suggestions for improving `reproducibility_check`

The following suggestions are drawn directly from running the module on all 435 code-bearing papers; each is grounded in a specific, confirmed observation from this run, not a general aspiration.

1. **Ship the common system libraries and header files in the Docker image.** The single largest avoidable cause of a failed install this run found was a package that needs a C or C++ development library the image did not contain: the GDAL/GEOS/PROJ development files behind the spatial packages (`rgdal`, `rgeos`, `gdalUtils`), and the compression and other headers behind several Bioconductor packages. This run had to build a second image with these added and run 58 papers again on it (A.7.5), after which every package the new headers covered installed. Adding these development libraries to the image Metacheck ships by default would let every future spatial or Bioconductor paper install its dependencies on the first attempt, rather than recurring as a per-paper failure.

2. **Give the Docker install backend the same CRAN Archive retry the process backend has.** When a package's current CRAN release fails to install but its last-published version in the CRAN Archive would install cleanly, the process backend (`repro_install_deps()`) retries against the Archive before giving up; the Docker backend (`repro_install_deps_docker()`) does not. Of the 90 packages that failed to install in exactly one paper each this run, 35% of the classified failures were a compilation failure and a further 6% were a package no longer on CRAN — some of which an Archive retry might recover. This would recover a share of the one-off install failures without any change to a paper's own code.

3. **Add a distinct outcome for a script that needs interactive input.** A script that calls `file.choose()` (an interactive file picker) or starts a blocking viewer such as `launch_shinystan()` cannot run unattended, but surfaces as an ordinary error or, worse, a script that sits until its time limit. The module already has an `interactive` reason for the clearest of these; broadening it to recognise a short list of known-interactive calls before execution, and distinguishing a script that produced no output before timing out, would let a report separate "this code cannot run unattended by design" from "this code is simply slow" — two very different findings for an author or reader.

4. **Extend the paper-by-paper qualitative review method of Appendices A.1–A.6 to `reproducibility_check`'s own output.** This appendix reports the rate and category of non-reproducibility across the 435 papers, but does not individually verify a sample of the failed scripts against their own paper's repository the way A.1–A.6 reviewed each `repo_check`/`data_check`/`code_check` disagreement. A systematic sample of the `other` category in particular (452 of the 2,248 failed scripts, the module's catch-all for an error that fits none of the named reasons) would likely surface further mechanically fixable causes, in the same style A.1–A.6 already found for the other modules.

## A.8 Three further reliability fixes to compressed-archive handling, and their effect on `data_archive`/`code_archived`/`code_download`

An eighth round of work returned to a structural limitation named repeatedly in earlier appendices but never itself directly fixed: `zip_peek()`'s inability to read a zip's contents without downloading it on Dryad and Figshare, both of which redirect a file's download URL to Amazon S3. Diagnosing and fixing this surfaced two further, closely related defects in the same download path, and reprocessing every paper the three fixes together could plausibly affect closed most, but not all, of the remaining `code_download` disagreement this comparison's own numbers above already reflect.

**`zip_peek()` failing on S3-backed hosts (scienceverse/metacheck#424).** `zip_peek()` reads a remote zip's table of contents with two requests: a `HEAD` to learn the file's total size, then a byte-range `GET` for the tail bytes holding the archive's central directory. Amazon S3 — the storage backend both Dryad's and Figshare's own download URLs redirect to — answers the size-only `HEAD` request with 403 but answers the byte-range `GET` normally (confirmed live: a `HEAD` against a real Dryad-hosted file returned 403, while a `Range: bytes=0-100` `GET` against the identical URL returned 206 with the file's true total size in its own `content-range` header). Because `.http_range_tail()`, the function `zip_peek()` calls to fetch the tail bytes, only sends its range request once `HEAD`'s size is known, a `HEAD` failure meant the byte-range request was never sent at all — not just for Dryad and Figshare but, confirmed the same way, for Harvard's Dataverse installation, another host redirecting to S3. Fix: fall back to a suffix range request (`Range: bytes=-<n>`) when `HEAD` fails, reading the total size from that response's own `content-range` header instead. Confirmed live before and after against nine archives sampled from this corpus (three each on Dryad, Figshare, and Zenodo): all six Dryad/Figshare archives returned `NULL` from `zip_peek()` before the fix and a correct, complete listing after it, while the three Zenodo archives (not S3-backed, and so unaffected by the underlying bug) listed correctly both times.

**`zip_peek()` never persisting its result across a restart (scienceverse/metacheck#427).** A separate, longstanding defect (`repo_info_cache()`) already exists specifically to persist a repository's *listing* (which files it has) to disk, since restarting an interrupted corpus run otherwise re-pays every repository's listing cost from scratch — a real problem previously severe enough to exhaust Dryad's own daily request quota (see that fix's own code comment, confirmed live 2026-09-08: 11 restarts of one 50-paper batch cost 440+ re-listing requests against a workload that genuinely needed a handful). `zip_peek()`'s own result — a zip's *contents*, a separate cost from the repository listing above it — had no equivalent: it was cached only in memory, for the life of one R process, so the same restart pattern silently re-peeked every zip already peeked, and `repo_check` and `data_check` each peeked the same zip independently (as two separate R processes in this project's own pipeline), doubling the cost again. Confirmed directly during this project's own corpus rerun (below): before this fix, four consecutive restarts each re-hit the same Dryad rate limit at the same early batch, at increasingly long waits (24.5, then 21.5, then 16 minutes remaining); after it, a restart at the same point in the run loaded every already-completed batch from disk in under 20 seconds and progressed past the previously-stuck batch with no rate-limit wait at all. Fix: persist `zip_peek()`'s result to disk the same way `repo_info_cache()` already does for a listing, gated on the same `cache = TRUE` argument.

**A silently discarded error in `download_repo_files()`'s archive-member fetch (scienceverse/metacheck#429).** Once `repo_check`'s zip-peek expansion lists a file living inside an archive (an "archive member," carrying `archive_url`+`archive_member` rather than its own `file_url`), `download_repo_files()` fetches it via a dedicated byte-range path (`.zip_fetch_members()`/`.zip_member_fetch()`), wrapped in a bare `tryCatch(..., error = function(e) NULL)` with no logging of any kind. A transient failure at this one step — a dropped connection, a timeout, a momentary host error — left `file_location` permanently `NA` with no warning, no log entry, and no record anywhere that a download had even been attempted, indistinguishable after the fact from a member the host genuinely cannot serve. This surfaced directly in this project's own corpus rerun: after #424 above let `repo_check`/`data_check` correctly list many more Dryad/Zenodo archive members than before, 24 papers whose code repository had previously never been detected at all (`mc_code_archived` `FALSE`) newly showed `mc_code_archived` `TRUE` but `mc_code_download` still `FALSE` — the code files were now correctly found, but never downloaded. Tracing one case in full (a small `.R` file inside a Dryad-hosted zip) confirmed the underlying fetch mechanism worked perfectly when called directly, with the paper's own exact saved row data and arguments, ruling out a logic bug; the corpus run's own 17,661-line warning log had no entry at all for this archive, this paper, or any of the other 23, confirming the failure really was silently discarded rather than merely unlogged elsewhere. Fix: record the specific error `.zip_fetch_members()` raises, the same way the ordinary `file_url` download path a few lines below already does, rather than discarding it.

**Reprocessing the 24 code-download regressions.** All 24 papers' `code_check` output was rerun against `dev` after #429's fix (`code_check` alone — `repo_check`'s listing and `data_check`'s own downloads were unaffected, confirmed directly: `mc_data_download` was already correctly `TRUE` for the papers where a data download was expected). 13 of 24 resolved immediately. The remaining 11 were rerun a second time with `skip_on_api_limit` set `FALSE` for this small, targeted rerun (unlike the corpus-wide default `TRUE`, whose own rationale — never blocking an unattended, hours-long, 1,861-paper run on a host's quota reset — does not apply to an 11-paper rerun, and, confirmed directly, was itself the reason these 11 still failed: their Dryad archive fetch had landed during a rate-limit window and been silently skipped rather than waited out, and waiting the quoted remaining time fetched the exact right file on the first attempt); 4 more resolved. The final 7 each printed a `download_repo_files()` retry-exhaustion message (`Failed to perform HTTP request`, `Re-run to retry: cached files are reused, only the missing files are fetched`) that — a `message()`/`cat()` call, not a `warning()` — this project's own rerun script's `warning =` handler could not catch or log, a message-routing gap distinct from #429's own fix and not itself corrected here; rerunning those 7 a third time, as the message itself instructed, resolved all 7. Every one of the original 24 papers now downloads successfully.

**Corpus-wide effect.** With these three fixes installed and the full 1,861-paper corpus rerun, sensitivity, specificity, and the number of papers newly entering each comparison (a repository or file that previously could not be evaluated at all now can be) all moved together in the direction these fixes targeted. `code_archived` agreement rose from 84.5% to `r pct1(results$code_archived$pct_agree/100)`% (sensitivity 60.1% to `r pct1(results$code_archived$sensitivity)`%), `any_readme` from 69.8% to `r pct1(results$any_readme$pct_agree/100)`% (sensitivity 59.6% to `r pct1(results$any_readme$sensitivity)`%), and `data_availability` from 83.3% to `r pct1(results$data_availability$pct_agree/100)`%. `code_download`'s own comparable count grew from 342 to `r results$code_download$n_both_coded` papers (50 papers whose code could not previously be evaluated for a download outcome at all — because it had never been detected as archived in the first place — now can be), and at that point only 2 disagreements remained across that larger, harder set (down from 24 when these three fixes began). After a later targeted rerun of every paper with an archive member that had not been downloaded, this time waiting out host rate limits (see the `code_download` results in the main text), `r results$code_download$n_disagree` `code_download` disagreement remains (`r pct1(results$code_download$pct_agree/100)`% agreement), a case where Metacheck is right and Cooper et al.'s coding missed the code. `zip_not_peeked` — the disagreement cause tracing directly to #424's own limitation — dropped to 0 as a recorded cause across every construct in this comparison's disagreement-cause categorization. The "compressed archive never opened" category among `data_archive`'s remaining under-coded papers (Appendix's own `data_archive_uncoded_papers.RData` analysis) fell from 70 papers to 12; the remainder now trace to distinct, already-documented causes (a code-only or documentation-only repository, a non-tabular file format `data_check` does not classify as data, or an image/GIS/3D file). Every previously-recorded disagreement in the corpus was re-reviewed the same way as every earlier round: 1,070 of 1,174 prior verdicts carried forward unmodified, because their underlying (paper, column, Cooper value, Metacheck value) triple was unchanged; every disagreement whose Metacheck-derived value changed, or which was newly surfaced, was reviewed from scratch (43 rows immediately after the corpus rerun above; 19 once the 24 papers' `mc_code_download` values were updated by the reprocessing described above and the comparison data rebuilt a second time) against the same evidence-source rule used throughout this manuscript (repository file listing and `repo_metadata` for `data_license`/`code_archived`/`any_readme`/`code_download`, the paper's own text for `data_availability`/`data_archive`). In the current worklist, `r review_status`.

**Archive downloads that failed during a corpus run, October 2026.** At this stage 25 `code_download` disagreements shared one cause: Metacheck found the paper's code files, all inside a zip archive on Dryad or Zenodo, but none of these archive members was downloaded in the corpus run, so `code_check` had no local file to inspect. The run recorded no reason for the failed downloads. A live recheck of these papers on 10 October 2026, with the same Metacheck version, retrieved a code file from each archive at exactly the size listed in the archive, so the code was downloadable and the failure was specific to that run rather than to the repositories. This is the same archive-member download pattern as scienceverse/metacheck#429. We reran Metacheck's repository, data, and code checks for all 191 papers with at least one archive member that had not been downloaded, this time recording the outcome of every download and waiting out host rate limits instead of skipping the file. The code of all 25 papers then downloaded. Host rate limits are the most plausible cause of the original failures, although that run recorded no reason: in the rerun, the last paper whose code still failed did so because Dryad refused the requests as too many (HTTP 429), and its code downloaded once the limit was waited out.

## A.9 A full, paper-by-paper review of every "unsupported repository, not detected" disagreement, and a full recheck of Appendix A.6's original categorization

```{r}
#| label: a9-recheck-230-setup

# Both ID lists below are a fixed historical snapshot from when this
# review was originally conducted, not a query against the live
# corpus -- deliberately, since the review itself (which DOI resolved,
# which platform was confirmed supported, which specific defect was
# diagnosed) is a one-time, dated piece of evidence, the same way
# Appendix A.1-A.6's defect narratives are. Since then, further fixes
# elsewhere in this project have corrected several of these exact
# papers' repo_check results, which removes them from
# repo_not_detected_categorization_data.csv entirely (a paper no longer
# showing a "repository not detected" disagreement has nothing left to
# categorize) -- confirmed directly: every one of this chunk's
# hardcoded ids now missing from the current CSV has
# mc_data_availability == TRUE, i.e. repo_check now finds a repository
# for it. Both tables below are filtered to the ids still present in
# the current CSV, so they render only real rows rather than blank ones
# for an id the CSV no longer carries; the prose states both counts
# (as originally reviewed, and as still present) rather than silently
# reporting only one.
a9_full <- read.csv("data/review/repo_not_detected_categorization_data.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
a9_full <- a9_full[!duplicated(a9_full$article_id), ]
a9_corrected_ids <- c(
  "10_1111_2041_210x_12894","10_1111_1365_2664_13806","10_1111_1365_2664_13077",
  "10_1111_2041_210x_13175","10_1111_2041_210x_13308","10_1111_1365_2435_14709",
  "10_1111_1365_2656_13910","10_1111_1365_2435_14241","10_1111_1365_2435_13955"
)
n_230_recheck_corrected <- length(a9_corrected_ids)
n_230_recheck_corrected_still_present <- sum(a9_corrected_ids %in% a9_full$article_id)
n_230_recheck_flagged <- 21L

# a9_cats: the 40-paper "not yet individually checked" set this section's
# opening paragraph and the full A.9 table both need -- built here, ahead of any
# prose in this section, so the inline `r nrow(a9_cats)` expressions
# below have a defined object to read at render time.
a9_new_ids <- c(
  "10_1111_1365_2664_13709","10_1002_pan3_10149","10_1111_1365_2745_12930",
  "10_1002_pan3_10307","10_1111_1365_2745_13067","10_1111_1365_2435_14226",
  "10_1002_2688_8319_12315","10_1111_1365_2745_14315","10_1111_2041_210x_14453",
  "10_1111_1365_2745_13529","10_1002_pan3_10743","10_1111_1365_2664_12991",
  "10_1002_2688_8319_12241","10_1111_1365_2745_13517","10_1111_1365_2435_13192",
  "10_1111_1365_2435_14550","10_1002_pan3_10677","10_1111_1365_2664_13065",
  "10_1111_1365_2745_13154","10_1111_1365_2745_12749","10_1111_1365_2435_14477",
  "10_1111_1365_2656_13970","10_1111_1365_2664_13892","10_1111_2041_210x_13110",
  "10_1111_1365_2745_14252","10_1111_1365_2664_14700","10_1111_1365_2656_13918",
  "10_1111_2041_210x_13463","10_1111_1365_2435_13550","10_1111_1365_2435_12874",
  "10_1111_1365_2664_14787","10_1111_1365_2656_14227","10_1111_1365_2745_13324",
  "10_1111_1365_2656_13272","10_1111_1365_2435_13791","10_1111_1365_2745_13849",
  "10_1111_1365_2435_14514","10_1111_1365_2435_13936","10_1111_1365_2664_13845",
  "10_1111_1365_2664_14229"
)
n_a9_new_ids_original <- length(a9_new_ids)
a9_cats <- a9_full[a9_full$article_id %in% a9_new_ids, ]
a9_cats <- a9_cats[match(a9_new_ids[a9_new_ids %in% a9_full$article_id], a9_cats$article_id), c("article_id", "category", "comment")]
names(a9_cats) <- c("Paper", "Category", "Evidence and verification")

# flextable already escapes LaTeX-special characters in cell text on its
# own (confirmed: "_" in these same free-text columns already renders
# correctly elsewhere in this document without any manual escaping) --
# manually escaping here as well double-escapes it. The one real problem
# case is a literal "\b" (a regex word-boundary, in free text describing
# Metacheck's own source code) that flextable's LaTeX writer does not
# treat as needing escaping; neutralise just that by inserting a
# zero-width separator so it can never be read as a control sequence,
# without touching any other character flextable already handles.
.break_stray_backslash <- function(x) gsub("\\\\", "\\\\ ", x)
a9_cats$`Evidence and verification` <- .break_stray_backslash(a9_cats$`Evidence and verification`)
```

Appendix A.6 categorized every "repository not detected" disagreement in the corpus, but `r n_a9_new_ids_original` of the `r n_unsupported_repo_and_mc_missed` papers whose only Cooper-coded `data_archive` label(s) fell outside Metacheck's supported-platform categories, and for which `repo_check` consequently found no repository at all, had not yet been individually checked one at a time when an earlier version of this manuscript's main text was written. This appendix documents that remaining review in full: each paper's own extracted data-availability text, the specific DOI or URL cited, whether it was live-verified to resolve, whether the cited platform is genuinely supported by Metacheck (checked directly against the vendored source in `code/data/reproducibility_check/vendor/metacheck/R/`, not inferred from this manuscript's own earlier prose, which had itself gone stale for at least one platform -- see below), and the final category assigned. All `r n_a9_new_ids_original` papers received a verdict at the time of this review; `r n_a9_new_ids_original - nrow(a9_cats)` have since had their underlying `repo_check` defect fixed by later work elsewhere in this project and no longer appear in the live disagreement set at all (confirmed: `repo_check` now finds a repository for every one of them), so @tbl-a9-full below shows the `r nrow(a9_cats)` that remain.

This review also surfaced a further risk worth checking directly rather than assuming away: Appendix A.6's original 230-row categorization was itself produced before the platform-support defects this review found (the stale 4TU/DANS assumptions, an incomplete dedicated-platform list, a missing DSpace-legacy host count), so any of those original 230 rows that happened to cite one of these same platforms could be mislabeled the same way. Rather than only check the platforms these specific bugs touch, every one of the original 230 rows was rechecked from scratch: each paper's own text was re-extracted directly from the corpus (paragraph-grouped, not sentence-truncated, avoiding the extraction bug documented earlier in this manuscript), every DOI and URL in that text was identified, and each one's host was checked directly against Metacheck's current supported-platform functions -- not against what an earlier comment claimed was or was not supported.

Of the 230, `r n_230_recheck_flagged` candidate citations resolved to a host now confirmed supported despite the row's original `UNSUPPORTED_REPO` label; after excluding false positives (a truncated GitHub URL with no repository path, a citation that names a genuinely unrelated, unsupported host despite superficially matching a regex), `r n_230_recheck_corrected` rows were corrected to `SUPPORTED_PLATFORM_BUG` or `SUPPORTED_PLATFORM_MISSED` at the time of this review. The corrected rows span three recurring patterns: a citation to a genuinely supported host that `repo_check` simply never queried (Dataverse, DataOne/KNB, Zenodo, standard-format Figshare), a supported platform cited via a URL format its matcher does not parse (a Figshare private share-link or collection URL), and a supported platform cited via a non-standard DOI prefix its prefix-matching does not recognise (an alternate Dryad EZID prefix, a non-standard Figshare prefix). None of the corrected rows involve a platform Metacheck genuinely cannot reach at all -- every correction is a detection defect on an already-supported platform, consistent with the pattern the original 40-paper review above found. `r n_230_recheck_corrected - n_230_recheck_corrected_still_present` of these `r n_230_recheck_corrected` papers have since had their underlying defect fixed by later work elsewhere in this project (the same `repo_check`-now-finds-it pattern as above) and no longer appear in the live disagreement set; @tbl-a9-corrected below shows the `r n_230_recheck_corrected_still_present` still remaining in it, with the full original set described narratively here regardless.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-a9-corrected
#| tbl-cap: "The rows from Appendix A.6's original 230-paper categorization corrected on full recheck, from `UNSUPPORTED_REPO` to a supported-platform category, still present in the current disagreement set."

a9_corrected_ids_present <- a9_corrected_ids[a9_corrected_ids %in% a9_full$article_id]
a9_corr_tab <- a9_full[a9_full$article_id %in% a9_corrected_ids_present, c("article_id", "category", "comment")]
a9_corr_tab <- a9_corr_tab[match(a9_corrected_ids_present, a9_corr_tab$article_id), ]
names(a9_corr_tab) <- c("Paper", "Category", "Evidence and verification")
flextable::flextable(a9_corr_tab) |>
  flextable::width(1, 1.3) |> flextable::width(2, 1.1) |> flextable::width(3, 4.6) |>
  flextable::fontsize(size = 7, part = "all")
```

Two platforms cited in this set turned out to be genuinely supported by Metacheck despite `repo_check` finding nothing, each traced to a specific, distinct defect rather than a missing backend. **4TU** (`data.4tu.nl`) has dedicated support (`archive-4tu.R`), and the DOI cited (`10.4121/uuid:04b25e70-ca3e-489f-9510-36385c1a4104`) live-resolves correctly to a real 4TU record. The ID-extractor correctly pulls the UUID from the DOI, but the live 4TU API lookup queries `data.4tu.nl/v2/articles/<uuid>`, which 404s, because 4TU's own DOI redirect resolves the identical record to a different, numeric article ID that the UUID does not match. This corrects an earlier, incorrect statement elsewhere in this manuscript (Appendix A.6) that this paper's 4TU fetch failure remained unresolved and should count as `UNSUPPORTED_REPO`; it is a supported-platform bug, not an unsupported platform. Since the rerun with Metacheck 0.3.3.11 (17 October 2026), Metacheck lists this record's files and finds the paper's data. **DANS EASY** is one of four separate subject-specific Dataverse installations DANS operates (archaeology/lifesciences/phys-techsciences/ssh), all sharing a single DOI prefix (`10.17026`). Metacheck's `.dataverse_host_from_doi()` resolves any DOI under this shared prefix to `archaeology.datastations.nl`, but the paper in this set cites a dataset actually hosted on `lifesciences.datastations.nl` -- a genuine Metacheck defect in DOI-to-host resolution for any DOI prefix shared across multiple Dataverse instances, not specific to DANS. A third paper cites the Knowledge Network for Biocomplexity (`knb.ecoinformatics.org`), a confirmed DataOne member node whose DOI live-resolves correctly; the specific reason `repo_check` did not detect it was not further root-caused within the scope of this review, so it is recorded as a supported-platform miss without a fully diagnosed cause, distinct from the two fully diagnosed bugs above.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-a9-full
#| tbl-cap: "Full paper-by-paper review of the 40 previously-unreviewed 'unsupported repository, not detected' disagreements: cited platform, live DOI/URL resolution status, and final category."

flextable::flextable(a9_cats) |>
  flextable::width(1, 1.3) |> flextable::width(2, 1.1) |> flextable::width(3, 4.6) |>
  flextable::fontsize(size = 7, part = "all")
```

Of these `r nrow(a9_cats)` papers, `r sum(a9_cats$Category == "UNSUPPORTED_REPO")` genuinely cite an unsupported platform, `r sum(a9_cats$Category == "NCBI_GENBANK")` cite a domain-specific bioinformatics accession outside `repo_check`'s scope, `r sum(a9_cats$Category %in% c("SUPPORTED_PLATFORM_BUG", "SUPPORTED_PLATFORM_MISSED"))` cite a platform Metacheck genuinely supports but failed to detect for the reasons described above, `r sum(a9_cats$Category == "TEXT_EXTRACTION_TRUNCATED")` had no usable citation captured in the paper's extracted text at all (either empty extraction or a citation cut off before any identifier appeared), `r sum(a9_cats$Category == "NO_REPO_DATA_RESTRICTED")` explicitly withheld their data with no repository to find, and `r sum(a9_cats$Category == "SOURCE_CITATION_ERROR")` paper's own published citation pointed to an internal, non-public address rather than a reachable repository. These per-paper counts feed directly into the corpus-wide reconciling numbers reported in the main text and into the totals of its table of reasons.

## A.10 Full paper-by-paper detail for every technical limitation identified in the full disagreement-population review

```{r}
#| label: a10-metacheck-limitations-load

# Generated directly from manual_repo_findability_audit_data.csv -- the same
# file the main text's table of reasons and five-cluster breakdown are computed
# from (see the full-317-audit-load chunk above). Every row here is one
# of the n_metacheck_limitation papers from that cluster; nothing below
# is hand-transcribed, so this table stays in sync with the CSV
# automatically whenever it is updated and this document is re-rendered.
# In the order the main text discusses them: text extraction first, then
# Metacheck's own code.
a10_labels <- c(
  EXTRACTION_GAP_DOI_GARBLED = "Text extraction: identifier corrupted by the PDF-to-text step",
  EXTRACTION_GAP_TEXT_MISSING = "Text extraction: no trace of the citation in the extracted text",
  SUPPORTED_PLATFORM_BUG = "Metacheck code: a defect in detecting or retrieving a supported repository",
  CLASSIFIER_ARCHIVE_NOT_EXPANDED = "Metacheck code: archive listed but never downloaded or opened",
  FILES_NOT_ENUMERATED = "Metacheck code: an R package's own source files excluded from the file listing"
)
stopifnot(setequal(names(a10_labels), metacheck_limitation_cats), length(a10_labels) == 5)

a10_tab <- full_audit[full_audit$root_cause_category %in% metacheck_limitation_cats,
                       c("paper_doi", "root_cause_category", "manual_why_metacheck_misses_it")]
a10_tab$root_cause_category <- a10_labels[a10_tab$root_cause_category]
# Order by category (in the same order as the main text discusses them),
# then by DOI within each category, for a predictable reading order.
a10_tab$.order <- match(a10_tab$root_cause_category, a10_labels)
a10_tab <- a10_tab[order(a10_tab$.order, a10_tab$paper_doi), ]
a10_tab$.order <- NULL
names(a10_tab) <- c("Paper (DOI)", "Category", "Why Metacheck misses it")
a10_tab$`Why Metacheck misses it` <- .break_stray_backslash(a10_tab$`Why Metacheck misses it`)
stopifnot(nrow(a10_tab) == n_metacheck_limitation)
```

@tbl-a10-limitations lists every one of the `r n_metacheck_limitation` papers in the main text's "technical limitation" cluster individually: its DOI, which of the five specific limitations (grouped into text extraction and Metacheck's own code, as in the main text) applies, and the evidence-based reasoning for that classification, generated directly from the same per-paper audit file (`manual_repo_findability_audit_data.csv`) the main text's numbers are computed from. Because the table is built programmatically from that file rather than transcribed by hand, it stays reconciled with the main text's counts automatically on every re-render (confirmed by the chunk above: the table's row count is checked against `n_metacheck_limitation` directly).

@tbl-a10-not-classified lists, in the same way, every one of the `r n_not_classified` papers in the main text's cluster of repositories that contain data or code Metacheck did not classify: `r n_not_fair_format` where the data or code were not shared in a FAIR format, and `r n_unsupported_format` where they are in a format Metacheck does not yet support.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-a10-not-classified
#| tbl-cap: "Full paper-by-paper detail for every paper whose repository contains data or code that Metacheck did not classify."

flextable::flextable(a10_nc_tab) |>
  flextable::width(1, 1.3) |> flextable::width(2, 1.5) |> flextable::width(3, 4.3) |>
  flextable::fontsize(size = 7, part = "all")
```

## A.11 What changed in the final run, why, and the consequences for the results

```{r}
#| label: a11-result-changes

targets::tar_load(result_changes, store = "_targets")
rc_pct <- result_changes$percentages
rc_cause <- result_changes$by_cause
rc_other <- result_changes$other_columns
rc_changes <- result_changes$changes
rc_on_request <- rc_other$n_papers[rc_other$column == "mc_on_request"]
rc_code_open <- rc_other$n_papers[rc_other$column == "mc_code_open"]
rc_toward <- sum(rc_changes$effect == "toward")
rc_away <- sum(rc_changes$effect == "away")
rc_new_agree <- sum(rc_changes$effect == "new_agreement")
rc_new_disagree <- sum(rc_changes$effect == "new_disagreement")
rc_still <- sum(rc_changes$effect == "still_disagrees")
rc_not_comparable <- sum(rc_changes$effect == "not_comparable")
rc_max_shift <- max(abs(rc_pct$final_pct_agree - rc_pct$earlier_pct_agree))
```

The results in this manuscript come from two runs. The `repo_check`, `data_check`, `code_check`, `open_practices` and ODDPub results come from one run on all 1861 papers with Metacheck commit e62da2e (version 0.4.2.1), after which 22 papers were run again with commit f7949c0, which holds fixes for faults found during that run. The `reproducibility_check` results come from a separate run, on the 435 of those papers that have runnable code, with commit f6aec07c (version 0.4.3.6) — described in A.7 — together with its two follow-up runs: 58 papers run again on an image with system header files added, and one paper run on the `dev` branch (0.4.3.13) after a fix for a fault that had stopped its check. Each paper's reproducibility result records which of these runs and which commit produced it. The repository, data and code results are unchanged from the earlier pass of this project described below; the reproducibility results are new to the final run.

The results of an earlier version of this project were a combination of several partial runs with older versions, the last of them with commit 610cd4f (version 0.3.3.11). This appendix compares the last of those earlier results, dated 18 October 2026, with the final results, for the columns that can be compared with Cooper et al.'s coding (the repository, data and code columns), to show whether the conclusions depend on the version of Metacheck. @tbl-a11-percentages shows they do not: no agreement percentage moved by more than `r round(rc_max_shift, 1)` percentage points.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-a11-percentages
#| tbl-cap: "Percentage agreement between Cooper et al. and Metacheck in the earlier and the final results, and the number of papers both coded."

rc_tab <- data.frame(
  Comparison = rc_pct$label,
  `Earlier %` = sprintf("%.1f", rc_pct$earlier_pct_agree),
  `Final %` = sprintf("%.1f", rc_pct$final_pct_agree),
  `Earlier n` = rc_pct$earlier_n_both_coded,
  `Final n` = rc_pct$final_n_both_coded,
  check.names = FALSE
)
flextable::flextable(rc_tab) |>
  flextable::width(1, 3.3) |> flextable::width(2:5, 0.8) |>
  flextable::fontsize(size = 8, part = "all")
```

In the columns compared with Cooper et al., `r result_changes$n_values` values changed, in `r result_changes$n_papers` of the 1861 papers. Of these values, `r rc_toward` moved from disagreement to agreement with Cooper et al. and `r rc_away` moved from agreement to disagreement. A further `r rc_new_agree + rc_new_disagree` could not be compared before, because one side had no answer, and can be now: `r rc_new_agree` agree and `r rc_new_disagree` disagree. Of the rest, `r rc_still` still disagree with a different value, and `r rc_not_comparable` cannot be compared in either version. @tbl-a11-causes gives the cause of each kind of change: the change in Metacheck, the commit that made it, and what it did to the results. @tbl-a11-changes lists every changed value.

Two causes change results for a reason other than a correction of Metacheck. `NOT_DOWNLOADED_ON_PURPOSE` is a decision for this run. For `NOW_DOWNLOADED`, the final run holds a saved copy of files that the earlier results do not, and we did not establish why the earlier runs had none.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-a11-causes
#| tbl-cap: "Causes of the changed values: the change in Metacheck, its commit, its consequence, and the number of papers (P) and values (V). T and A: values that moved to or away from agreement with Cooper et al. N+ and N-: values that could not be compared before and now agree or disagree."

rc_cause_tab <- data.frame(
  Cause = rc_cause$cause,
  Commit = rc_cause$metacheck_commit,
  Mechanism = rc_cause$mechanism,
  Consequence = rc_cause$consequence,
  P = rc_cause$n_papers,
  V = rc_cause$n_values,
  T = rc_cause$n_toward,
  A = rc_cause$n_away,
  `N+` = rc_cause$n_new_agreement,
  `N-` = rc_cause$n_new_disagreement,
  check.names = FALSE
)
flextable::flextable(rc_cause_tab) |>
  flextable::width(1, 0.9) |> flextable::width(2, 0.55) |> flextable::width(3, 2) |>
  flextable::width(4, 1.05) |> flextable::width(5:10, 0.25) |>
  flextable::fontsize(size = 6, part = "all")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-a11-changes
#| tbl-cap: "Every changed value in a column compared with Cooper et al."

rc_short <- function(x) {
  x <- gsub("GitHub, GitLab, Codeberg or similar platform", "GitHub", x, fixed = TRUE)
  x <- gsub("Other repo/database", "Other", x, fixed = TRUE)
  ifelse(is.na(x), "missing", x)
}
rc_change_tab <- data.frame(
  Paper = rc_changes$article_id,
  Column = rc_changes$column,
  Earlier = rc_short(rc_changes$earlier_value),
  Final = rc_short(rc_changes$final_value),
  Effect = rc_changes$effect,
  Cause = rc_changes$cause
)
flextable::flextable(rc_change_tab) |>
  flextable::width(1, 1.4) |> flextable::width(2, 0.9) |> flextable::width(3:4, 1.05) |>
  flextable::width(5, 0.8) |> flextable::width(6, 1.2) |>
  flextable::fontsize(size = 6.5, part = "all")
```

Columns that are not compared with Cooper et al. changed for more papers. The largest changes do not reflect a change in what was found: `mc_on_request` went from missing to FALSE for `r rc_on_request` papers, because every paper now gets a row in `open_practices`. `mc_code_open` went from TRUE to FALSE for `r rc_code_open` papers, because only a capital R now counts as a word for code, so a statistic such as r(68) = .58 no longer makes a sentence a statement about code. @tbl-a11-other-columns lists these columns.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-a11-other-columns
#| tbl-cap: "Changes in columns that are not compared with Cooper et al."

rc_other_tab <- data.frame(Column = rc_other$column, Papers = rc_other$n_papers,
                           Commit = rc_other$metacheck_commit, Mechanism = rc_other$mechanism)
flextable::flextable(rc_other_tab) |>
  flextable::width(1, 1.2) |> flextable::width(2, 0.5) |> flextable::width(3, 1.3) |> flextable::width(4, 3.6) |>
  flextable::fontsize(size = 7, part = "all")
```

The final results keep two limitations that these comparisons brought to light. First, `repo_check` removes the folders of an R package at a repository's root when any file classified as data or code lies outside them, on the assumption that the package is a dependency bundled into a study's repository. In the saved GitHub listings this removes files from 46 packages in 41 papers, among them the authors' own package in 10.1111/2041-210X.13437, where only the files of a documentation website lie outside it. Adding the removed files back to the final results, in a simulation that is not part of this pipeline and covers GitHub listings only, changes the answer on whether code is archived for one paper (agreement falls from 87.9% to 87.8%), the agreement on the code platform from 78.0% to 77.8%, and on the data platform from 90.3% to 90.2%. We therefore left the rule unchanged. Second, because `.json` files count as data, a configuration file such as `package.json` can make a software repository count as holding data: 11 papers have such a file among their data files, and in 2 papers all data files are JSON files.
